  • Recent findings suggest that keeping your home safe these days takes more than a deadbolt and a dog with a menacing bark.
  • Outdoor security cameras in particular are your best bet to prevent break-ins.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Recent findings suggest that keeping your home safe these days takes more than a deadbolt and a dog with a menacing bark. Installing a few security cameras around your property is an easy and surprisingly cost-effective way to level up your home security, adding watchful eyes that track comings and goings 24/7. Until relatively recently, the only options for personal home security were comprehensive (and expensive) systems that were installed and monitored by security professionals. Now, you can set up your own cameras and home security system that saves you cash without sacrificing performance.

Outdoor security cameras in particular are your best bet to prevent break-ins. According to Security.org, simply having a clearly visible camera or security device on your property serves as a strong deterrent for trespassers. Outdoor security cameras are equipped with features found in indoor security cameras like high-definition video, night vision, two-way audio, and more. In addition to this, they come equipped with outdoor-specific features like weather-resistant exteriors, sound detection, and integrated motion-activated spotlights.

For this guide, we got our hands on the most promising options from well-established brands including Arlo, Wyze, Ring, and Eufy and tested them at our homes and offices. Read on below to learn about the best outdoor security cameras we recommend, along with expert advice to help you choose the right option for your home and budget.

Sources indicate that one quick note before we dive in: It’s increasingly key to pick security gear that’s compatible with whatever smart home system you already have. For example, Amazon makes it easy to pull up a live feed from your Ring camera(s) on an Echo Show or Fire TV and has designed its products to more seamlessly connect with its other smart home devices. Same goes for Google products. If you already have a few items from a major smart home brand, consider buying gear that will be as compatible as possible with it.

More Home Improvement Stories: Best Retractable Awnings ● The Popular Mechanics 2025 Yard & Garden Awards ● Best Solar-Powered Outdoor Lights.

It has been revealed that we selected our recommendations based on a round of substantial testing: We installed these cameras outdoors, and used them to survey our homes for weeks, and in some cases months. We watched them as they watched our properties, as they endured a wide spectrum of outdoor conditions including snow and rain.

We tested and compared their basic video recording functionality, evaluating them on clarity, field of view, and weather resistance as well as any special features they offer like spotlights, solar charging, sirens, and more. Some of the cameras on this list were tested in outdoor settings for months, facing a wide spectrum of outdoor conditions including snow and rain.

We also tested their more nuanced security and tech features, including motion detection notifications, AI recognition of animals and packages, two-way audio conversations, and digital borders, among others. These features were considered as well as the cost, if any, associated with buying access to all of them.

We recommended the Wyze Outdoor Cam V2 ahead of testing, based on its low price, solid specs, and the past performance of other Wyze cameras that we've tested.

The Arlo Essential XL stands out for its user-friendly design, durable exterior, and of course, its clear video quality—all for a fair price. It's completely wireless, which means you can mount it anywhere around your home without worrying about power and wiring complications.

It excels as a 24/7 outdoor cam, with features like color night vision that improves the clarity of nighttime footage. During testing, we were impressed by its resolution in low light, as well as its accurate motion detection. It provides real-time alerts directly to your smartphone, and will let you check a live feed to observe any suspicious activity live as it happens.

Industry observers note that you can also program the integrated spotlight to automatically flash on when someone is within visual range. It's a great deterrent against potential robberies, and lets you leave the house without leaving a porch light on.

While this cam has solid features without a subscription, an Arlo Secure subscription adds cloud storage for your video footage, as well as additional target recognition and home security features, for $96 to $300 per year.

Arlo Essential XL Security Camera Review.

Sources indicate that few options balance price and quality as well as this affordable option from Wyze. The battery-operated Wyze Outdoor V2 camera can be mounted anywhere. New buyers should pick up the starter kit, which includes a base unit that allows you to expand your system with up to four cameras.

Though it's the most affordable on the list, it still offers a lineup of powerful features including motion-sensing technology that detects both body heat and movement, reducing the number of potential false alarms drastically.

The Wyze is also quite flexible for storage options with the camera capable of online cloud storage as well as localized storage on a microSD card.

It has been revealed that solar-powered cameras, while power-efficient, present extra setup challenges. Most of the time, the panel is attached to the body of the camera, so you need to need find to camera positions with a good field of view and get good sun exposure. Depending on the layout of your home and the surrounding area, that may lead to less-than-ideal placements, which create holes in your surveillance.

The Tapo MagCam solves this issue with a detachable solar panel, so you can keep it connected when it's effective, or remove and mount it higher above the camera to get more sun. It features a 13-foot extension cord, so you have a good amount of slack to move it to an open, sunshiny space.

Industry observers note that test Editor Bradley Ford mounted his test camera in a semi-shaded area, then set up the solar panel in direct sunlight. Despite the fact that he was testing at the end of 2025, when there was significantly less daily sunlight, the battery never dipped below 80 percent charge. In the warmer weather, the camera typically sat at 100 percent.

Recent findings suggest that in addition, Ford preferred that the MagCam relied on local storage. "One of the things we like best is that there is no need for a subscription to access activation videos," Ford noted. "They’re all stored locally on a Micro SD card in the camera. However, if you wish to pay for cloud storage, that option is also available.".

This specific kit comes with a camera, solar panel, and mount, however Tapo offers others with two or three cameras as well.

Sources indicate that our previous pick in this category, the Ring Floodlight Cam Wired Plus, was a terrific outdoor security camera that featured a dual-LED floodlight. The newly introduced Ring Floodlight Cam Wired Pro builds on that solid design with extra features, including support for dual-band WiFi and a “bird’s-eye view” feature that tracks a recorded subject as they move within the camera’s view, showing it on a top-down layout of the area.

The camera’s 1080p video resolution and 140-degree field of view are the same as the previous model, but image quality is enhanced with high dynamic range (HDR) support, which improves visibility in both low light and extremely bright conditions.

The lights themselves are also quite bright, 2000 lumens each, and the fixtures are adjustable so you can angle the light as you please.

The Ring Floodlight Cam Wired Pro also features two-way audio support, with a 110-decibel siren that sounds when the system detects motion. It also offers customizable motion zones and 3D- motion radar for you to tailor to your property.

A word of warning: We found the wired installation was fairly difficult, so we recommend hiring an electrician unless you're experienced with wiring and up for a challenge.

Unlike any other outdoor security camera on our list, this option from Tactacam does not require a WiFi connection. Instead, it connects to cellular towers and works similarly to your smartphone. This makes the camera perfect for homes in remote locations.

The security camera does require a monthly subscription for access to on-demand videos and photos that are stored in the cloud, but prepares start at just 5 bucks a month.

In a recent development, the device works with AA batteries or a rechargeable battery pack. In our testing, we took anywhere from two to 10 pictures a day and the pack lasted about three to four months before needing to be recharged.

Industry observers note that in practice, the security camera is great at sensing motion more than 100 feet away, so it could potentially double as a nature cam. It lacks some of the features other, similarly priced models on this list have, but the biggest drawback is that the field of view is only about 50 feet wide.

The Arlo floodlight has everything we love from our top pick, including Arlo's superior app and software, but adds on a large floodlight, as well as a need for wired power.

As with the Arlo Essential XL, you get quality motion detection software and color night vision. Spring for Arlo Secure, and you get AI target recognition that can point out passing cars or faces, and highlight packages.

According to recent reports, the floodlight also has some interesting features: Each light is individually adjustable, so you can angle them for the best possible coverage. That includes creative solutions like angling one light toward your back door, while pointing the other toward the steps leading to your back porch. It's a small touch, but a very appreciated one. It also includes a loud, 110-decibel siren.

If you're looking for a low-maintenance outdoor security camera system, eufy's S330 "eufycam 3" is a dynamic wireless option that supports solar charging and doesn't require professional installation.

Industry observers note that once installed and set up, we did not have to take either of the cameras down for recharging once over months of use. The solar panels kept them perpetually charged as long as they got exposure to a few hours of sunlight per day.

Industry observers note that it was similarly easy to connect the cameras to the greater home security. The outdoor cameras works through the home hub which after initial installation using an ethernet cable, works comfortably through your home WiFi. The cameras can then be set up anywhere within several hundred feet of the hub without losing connection.

A massive benefit we also loved is the camera system requires no monthly subscription to access its features. This includes AI-powered face recognition, customizable activity zones, and of course, motion detection.

In a recent development, the only drawback for this camera set is the placement of the solar panels. While the panels being integrated directly on top of the camera makes it less cumbersome, it also means you need to install them in a spot with direct sunlight or they won't properly charge.

The Reolink Argus 4 Pro gives you a sweeping 180-degree field of view, which allows you to cover large open spaces with as few cameras as possible. Properly positioned, you can achieve a near-complete view of an area with just two cameras.

Industry observers note that this 4K camera features a dual-lens design that covers larger areas without blind spots or fishbowl-style warping. You'd think that might lead to complications with position or usage, but we found it easy to operate.

It features discrete solar panels for power, which allows for more placement flexibility: For example, you can install the camera under a ledge or rooftop, then secure the solar panel above, where it will get direct sun. That makes it easier to get the perfect shot and optimal power.

According to recent reports, in terms of storage, the Argus 4 Pro records footage locally and connects to a home hub. You don't have to pay a monthly fee for cloud storage or additional features. Simply turn it on, connect it the hub, and in theory, it should run without problem in perpetuity.

There are two types of consumer-grade home security cameras: wireless battery-powered cameras that you can set up easily nearly anywhere, but require you to occasionally replace batteries, and wired models that connect directly to your home's electrical system.

Recent findings suggest that wired cameras are generally more expensive and require an electrician's help unless you're comfortable with home wiring, but require far less maintenance once they're installed. Their placement is also restricted to locations where you can wired them in.

In a recent development, battery-powered cameras, by contrast, are only restricted by the range of your WiFi router. Of course, you'll need to access them every few months to replace their batteries. Some models feature solar panels, giving you renewable energy, but panels also impose some placement restrictions. (Namely, access to sunlight).

Wired cameras do fall short of battery-powered models in one niche scenario—when the power goes out. Unlike, say, wired smoke or carbon monoxide detectors, which have reliable battery backup, you can't count on a wired security camera to provide surveillance footage during an extended period of time if there's a power failure. It varies from model to model, but most wired cameras can only last for 30 minutes to, at most, a few hours before they go dark.

To avoid recording 24/7, which wastes power and storage space, outdoor security cameras usually feature motion sensors that trigger recording whenever there’s activity. Many cameras will also an alert to your companion app whenever they start recording.

Most cameras give you the ability to calibrate the motion sensor by setting motion zones in spots where you expect frequent false alarms, like a sidewalk. Others offer smart features that can differentiate between people, animals, and vehicles. You should also have the ability to customize your notifications, so you’ll only receive an alert in certain situations, like if it detects a person.

It has been revealed that furthermore, some cameras feature microphones, enabling audio detection, which can trigger recording and alerts based on nearby sounds that may be out of view (like a window breaking). Audio detection is a useful extra layer in a few specific situations, like when a single camera can’t cover the entire side of your home, but may also lead to more nuisance alerts. If you decide to use one, we recommend customizing your audio alert sensitivity if possible so you aren’t constantly getting notified when the neighbor’s dog barks.

The best outdoor security cameras record video in "Full HD" (1920 x 1080p) resolution, which captures enough detail to identify facial features or a car’s license plate. More expensive cameras record at higher resolutions, such as 2K or "Quad HD" (2560 x 1440p) or 4K Ultra HD (3840 x 2160) video, which deliver better detail. While higher resolution may help, 1080p video is usually clear enough to give you more than enough information in most situations.

According to recent reports, your camera’s field of view (FOV) is just as important as its resolution. Field of view refers to how wide of an angle the lens is and therefore, how much of your yard or porch is in view. With a wider FOV, your camera can see a wider area around your property, providing more coverage. For the best results, we recommend a model with a field of view between 130 and 180 degrees.

Recent findings suggest that many outdoor cameras also feature an integrated spotlight that can illuminate the surroundings if motion is detected, improving visibility in low-light situations. A spotlight also acts as a deterrent by making potential intruders more visible. Similarly, the majority of outdoor cameras offer some kind of night vision feature, which uses infrared (IR) lights to record a high-contrast black and white video in the dark. Top-of-the-line cameras are capable of recording standard video in low light, minimizing the need for night vision.

In a recent development, there’s no point in recording camera footage if you can’t store it for when you need it. Many manufacturers offer free cloud storage for a limited time—typically seven days–after which video is overwritten with new recordings. You can always download and save that footage, so long as you do during that initial window.

If you want to save your footage for a longer period, there are a couple of options. Many companies provide additional cloud storage for a subscription fee. There are also cameras that feature a microSD card slot for storing footage locally. This does require a bit of extra maintenance in the form of occasionally removing the card and either deleting or downloading the recorded data to free up more space on the card.

Industry observers note that if you’re concerned with privacy, be aware that cloud footage is generally kept on a manufacturer’s servers, which can be stolen if the company’s digital security is breached. Some companies may also use or share data from stored recordings in ways you might not anticipate. For example, Amazon has shared footage from Ring cameras to law enforcement without customers’ permission on many occasions. While storing locally requires more legwork, it is definitely the most secure option for privacy-conscious homeowners.

Security cameras are more than just their features. Nearly all security cameras are built to connect with other smart home devices. So, before buying any specific option, make sure it is compatible with the devices you already own. For example, Amazon makes it easy to pull up a live feed from your Ring camera(s) on an Echo Show or Fire TV. There are many brands that work with the majority of the smart home software available such as Apple, Google Nest, and Ring. Some have limited functionality on other smart home software systems outside of their brand, but still work with them. Furthermore, most security camera brands require a monthly subscription to gain full access to many of their features. These monthly subscriptions range in price and overall necessity with some basically essential to operate the cameras and store footage in the cloud while others are designed as a bonus add-on to the base product. Prior to purchase, make sure to take a close look at both the smart home compatibility as well as what comes with and without the monthly subscription service.

In a recent development, most of the outdoor security cameras we recommend are sold individually or as part of a larger set. The number of cameras you need for your property will vary, based on your home security plan and how much camera coverage you want. A well-installed camera with a wide field of view can cover an crucial and vulnerable area on your property, such as a back door or garage.

That noted, even a small home will need at least a few cameras to achieve full coverage on every ground-level door and window. You may need multiple cameras to reveal tricky blind spots created by corners, lawn features, and anything else that might impede a single camera position.

Recent findings suggest that don't freak out about needing a fleet of surveillance gear, though. Not everyone wants or needs to have every single square inch of their property under constant watch. It’s up to you to decide where you want an extra eye. The key thing is to make sure you know what you need before making a purchase.

It has been revealed that of course. There are no features of an outdoor security camera that would prevent it from working inside. That said, many companies make indoor cameras that are cheaper, and may feature a stand or mounting options that make more sense for blending in with your home or office.

According to recent reports, you should always be careful when considering home security. Over the years, there have been multiple reports of strangers accessing live video feeds and recorded videos from home security cameras.

Sources indicate that luckily, there are simple ways to protect yourself. As with other devices, adhering to digital security best practices, such as keeping your smart home devices’ firmware up to date, creating a strong password and activating two-factor authentication wherever possible, will help prevent a breach.

You may also have concerns about who has access to video that’s stored in the cloud. Most companies ask for permission to review recordings for research and development purposes. Depending on the company, this request often comes in the form of an “opt-in” setting in the camera app, though some may turn it on by default unless you “opt out.”.

Sources indicate that some may also share recordings with law enforcement. In some cases, they will only do so when compelled by a search warrant. A couple manufacturers, specifically Amazon (Ring) and Google (Nest), have noted they will provide footage without a warrant if law enforcement claims it is an emergency.

Latest Update: At the Races: Regional realignment

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1907 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.
  • Last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout.
  • One Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.

Last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout. Maine’s Susan Collins, Fresh England's last GOP senator, lost her seat to Democrat Troy Jackson, leaving former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, who just won a House seat, as the lone Republican headed to Congress from the region. (The picture was a bit brighter at the state level, where GOP Govs. Phil Scott of Vermont and Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire were both reelected.).

One Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era. In an opinion piece in The Boston Globe, consultant Kristin Tate urged Latest England Republicans to focus on fiscal discipline and recognize that “independence from national party leadership can be a political asset, not an act of betrayal.”.

After all, as the midterm election results remind us, no political realignment lasts forever.

Three decades ago, there were plenty of moderate Democrats from Southern states serving in Congress, governor’s mansions and even the White House. But in the years since Bill Clinton's exit from the political stage, Democrats have largely written off the South.

According to recent reports, which is partly why last week’s Democratic wins in the Carolinas, Georgia and, perhaps most notably, Mississippi were so stunning. All the elements that powered the party to victory nationally – disillusionment with Donald Trump, a rise in economic populism and hunger for change – played a role in the South as well.

But other factors were unique to a region that has seen renewed attempts to dilute Black political power with the redrawing of House districts to favor the GOP.

The Republican redistricting gambit in Southern states did not fully yield the desired results and seems to have helped galvanize Black voters and their allies, powering Democrats to unlikely victories.

It’s too soon to say whether the GOP’s reduced hold on the South represents a temporary blip or an enduring shift.

But Joe Trippi, a longtime Democratic strategist who advised candidates in Alabama and Florida this year, has a message for his party: “We need to invest in the South.”.

#MSSEN: Democrat Scott Colom defeated GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction and the first in his party to win a Senate seat in the Magnolia State since 1982.

Industry observers note that tar Heel tidal wave: Democrats in North Carolina have picked up at least five House seats, a striking development given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Prior to last week, no House Republican incumbent had lost a general election in the state since Republicans won control of the redistricting process more than a decade ago. And the Democratic gains could grow: In the 5th District, former journalist Chuck Hubbard narrowly leads 11-term Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx, and in the 3rd District, former state Rep. Raymond Smith holds a razor-thin edge over Republican Rep. Greg Murphy. The Associated Press had not called either race at publication time, though Murphy has conceded.

It has been revealed that republicans pick campaign chairs: Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack will be the chairs of Republicans’ respective campaign committees for the 2028 cycle. GOP lawmakers held their leadership elections Tuesday, as our colleagues Savannah Behrmann and John T. Bennett reported. Senate Republicans are sticking with South Dakota’s John Thune to lead them in the next Congress, while House Republicans picked former Freedom Caucus Chair Jim Jordan as their leader.

Industry observers note that redistricting doubts: Maryland could be getting a new congressional map after voters approved a constitutional amendment that would clear the way for new lines in 2028. Our colleague Victor Feldman has more on the result and other election-related ballot measures across the country. But it’s not clear how many other states may look to redistrict next cycle after Republican efforts over the past 18 months largely didn’t pay off in last week’s elections.

Run the table: With Rep. Darren Soto winning a sixth term in Florida, no Democratic incumbent lost reelection to a Republican this year. Soto’s win in a redrawn district also meant that Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had targeted under a new congressional map.

Sources indicate that california contest: Rep. Ken Calvert defeated fellow Republican Rep. Young Kim in a rare member-versus-member contest for a redrawn Southern California seat that turned acrimonious. Republicans are poised to hold just four House seats in the Golden State after Democrats made good on five pickup opportunities under a new congressional map.

Cheesecake Factory caucus: The latest episode of the Political Theater podcast, hosted by Roll Call editor-in-chief Jason Dick, breaks down how candidates in both parties fared in counties where The Cheesecake Factory operates, after the popular chain restaurant became something of a side character in the closing weeks of the midterm campaign.

Back to school: Newly elected members of Congress are on Capitol Hill this week for freshman orientation, an experience Massachusetts Rep.-elect Dan Koh told our colleague Nina Heller is “like high school – but it’s fun high school.” The incoming lawmakers took their class photo Thursday morning and will get to pick their Capitol Hill offices after next week’s famed lottery, Nina writes.

Tracking the count: As of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time Thursday, House Democrats had flipped 44 seats, while Republicans had picked up three. Twelve races remain uncalled, including a pair in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. On the Senate side, Democrats have flipped eight seats, with only Alaska’s race still undecided.

Recent findings suggest that guv update: Democrats flipped at least five governorships last week and will hold a majority of governor’s mansions next year. Two gubernatorial races remain uncalled by the AP: Kansas, where Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher is narrowly ahead of Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson, and Alaska, where Democratic former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is just below the 50 percent threshold to win the election outright. In territorial elections, Republicans flipped the governor’s office in Guam while voters in the Northern Mariana Islands will pick their next governor in a Nov. 20 runoff.

It has been revealed that #TNSEN: Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected Tennessee governor last week, is poised to pick her Senate successor. According to the Nashville Banner, the short list includes Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, a former professional wrestler, Reps. Tim Burchett and Chuck Fleischmann, and Tennessee Deputy Gov. Stuart McWhorter.

2028 on the brain: A handful of House Democrats are already considering 2028 Senate bids, according to Axios, including Kansas’ Sharice Davids, North Carolina’s Don Davis and Pennsylvania’s Chris DeLuzio.

Sources indicate that senator Morrison? Minnesota Rep. Kelly Morrison is earning buzz as a potential appointee to fill the Senate seat that Democrat Amy Klobuchar is vacating to become governor, Semafor reports. House Democrats aren’t likely to be as concerned about open seats as their Republican counterparts were in recent years, given the size of the incoming Democratic majority.

AOC’s future: Progressive activists have launched a new organization to encourage New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president in 2028. Meanwhile, Axios reports that Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with the digital fundraising firm she’s worked with for several years and has brought on the same firm that Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders used during his two presidential campaigns.

Women lead: Shirley Emehelu is New Jersey’s new lieutenant governor after Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill picked her to succeed Dale Caldwell, who resigned in September amid sexual harassment allegations and other ethical lapses. New Jersey is now one of five states to have women in both the governor’s and lieutenant governor’s offices, along with Massachusetts, Arkansas, Iowa and Virginia. Iowa will come off the list next year after an all-male Democratic ticket swept this year’s gubernatorial race, though five other states elected women to both offices last week.

Congress will once again be filled with losers – i.e, latest members who have lost previous bids for elected office. Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections returns to his biennial tradition as he runs down the latest list of “losers.”.

Industry observers note that ducking the wave: Democrats notched significant wins in unexpected places, but one state grew redder after last week’s elections. The Upcoming York Times checks in with voters in South Dakota, where the GOP won all nine statewide elections.

Sources indicate that here come the MBAs: Democrats with corporate connections were among the winners in last week’s elections, countering the idea that candidates with serious business credentials have struggled within the party, The Wall Street Journal reports. The field of 19 winners with M.B.A. degrees includes Costco board member Helena Buonanno Foulkes, who won the Rhode Island governor’s race, and Paige Cognetti, a Goldman Sachs alum who flipped a House seat in Pennsylvania.

Sources indicate that how Ricketts did it: Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts’ election night success was one of the few bright spots for the GOP. Ricketts fended off a challenge from independent Dan Osborn by painting him as a Democrat, questioning his authenticity and highlighting leaked audio of his comments denigrating Trump voters, writes the Nebraska Examiner.

Was it necessary? California redrew its congressional map to favor Democrats in response to Texas taking a similar step to boost the GOP. But some are questioning whether the state needed to cast aside its independent redistricting commission to rejigger the lines, given the scale of Democrats’ wins. “What they were literally saying is, ‘Let’s undo democracy to protect democracy,’” Lincoln Project co-founder Mike Madrid told CalMatters. “There’s something very Orwellian about it.”.

Song of the cycle: The New York Times reviews “Talafreako,” an unlikely viral anthem celebrating the newly elected Democratic senator from Texas.

History does rhyme: An opinion piece in The (Charleston) Post & Courier argues that the win by Democratic Sen.-elect Annie Andrews is the latest in a long line of cases in which South Carolina voters bucked the idea of party bosses picking their leaders.

The man behind the grill: The Latest York Times profiles Russ Hudson, the Mississippi man in Colom’s now-legendary “Pick another protein” ad.

That was the last time Democrats won 11 House seats in North Carolina.

According to recent reports, as of Thursday afternoon, they appear on track to match that number. They’ve already won nine seats – a mark they last cleared in the 1982 midterms – and they’re narrowly ahead in two more races.

If those leads hold, Democrats' 11-member delegation would look much different than the one sworn in some 66 years ago in 1961. Tar Heel Democrats taking office in January would include four women, six Black members and one Hispanic member.

Their 11 representatives (out of 12) in the 87th Congress were all white men who consistently voted to uphold racial segregation and oppose major federal civil rights legislation.

Vote counting in Alaska is expected to conclude by Wednesday, Nov. 18, the targeted date for ranked choice tabulations in races in which no candidate took more than 50 percent of the vote. As of Thursday, Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in the Senate race, though she’s below the 50 percent threshold.

Meanwhile, Democrats are gathering in Denver beginning Thursday to celebrate their historic wins and plot their next steps.

One of the most prominent features on the Moon is one we canât regularly see, at least not completely. The South Pole-Aitken (SPA) basin is one of the largest, oldest, and deepest impact craters on the Moon, and until recently weâve only been able to observe it from afar - and even then only when we sent orbiters around to the far side, which is never in direct line of sight with the Earth. Recently China has been busily sending landers and rovers to the site, and a fresh paper, published in Science Advances, details the actual samples returned to Earth by the Changâe-6 mission and combines them with the in-situ data from the Changâe-4 mission and rover. Those details combine to form a complete geological history of the major impacts that formed the basin, and some insight into the age of other impact craters scattered throughout the solar system.

According to recent reports, A sense of scale and time helps in understanding the SPA. Itâs roughly 2,200 kilometers across, making it similar in length to the north-south axis of mainland China. And it runs up to 10 kilometers deep, much deeper than any comparable land-based feature on Earth. For a long time, astronomers and planetary scientists have been debating how old it is, with dates ranging from 4.35 billion years ago to around 4.2 billion. That discrepancy is part of what the new paper hopes to solve, but thereâs another larger discrepancy it hopes to solve as well.

Industry observers note that the two halves of the Moon - the one that faces us and the one facing away - appear very different in terms of their features. The nearside is covered in smooth, dark plains called âmariaâ, whereas the far side has many more craters, with almost no volcanic plains and a thick layer of crust sitting on top. This difference, known as the âlunar dichotomy,â has stumped scientists for years. To solve it, many have turned to the SPA.

But the main crater isnât the only one in the area. Various smaller craters have formed overlapping the main one, including the Von KÃ¡rmÃ¡n crater (where Changâe-4 landed with its Yutu-2 rover) and the 490-kilometer-wide Apollo basin, where Changâe-6 landed and that was created by a separate impact.

Industry observers note that crucially, those impacts created different types of magnesium-rich igneous rocks. One type, found by Changâe-4 in the Von KÃ¡rmÃ¡n crater, is known as moderately magnesium-rich norite. It crystallized directly from the vast sea of molten rock generated when the SPA-forming asteroid slammed into the Moon. Over millions of years, the lava lake this created cooled, and the minerals separated out into layers. Later impacts then pushed the solid rocks up to the peaks of newly formed craters, and eventually another impact known as the Finsen impact blasted pieces of that cooled lava lake into Von KÃ¡rmÃ¡n crater for Changâe-4 to find.

Sources indicate that another type of rock held even higher levels of magnesium. It was created via a process called magnesium-suite magmatism. When the SPA impact broke the Moonâs crust, the magma from its then liquid interior broke into the crust, cooling underneath its top layer. Later, the impact that created the Apollo basin pushed those now cooled materials up into its western peak ring, and then another impact that created whatâs now known as the Chaffee S crater blasted pieces of rock directly into the path of plains where Changâe-6 collected them billions of years later.

Fraser talks about the Chang'e-6 mission collecting lunar samples.

Combining the data from Changâe-4âs rover with data from around a gram of the 2kg returned by the Changâe-6 mission, while adding a sprinkle of computer simulations, the research team reconstructed a timeline of the early bombardment history of the Moon. The main feature was when SPA was created around 4.34 billion years ago, only a few hundred million years after the solar system itself formed.

It has been revealed that the Apollo basin seemed to have been formed around 4.2 billion years ago, definitively answering why previous estimates of the SPA itself ranged from 4.35 billion years to 4.2 billion or so. Even later, around 3.87 billion years ago, another massive collision created what is now known as the Orientale basin, and after it came smaller impacts like Finsen and Chaffee S, which showered the entire region with debris that mixed the crust rocks in with the soil that formed on the Moon over hundreds of millions of years.

While itâs great to know the Moonâs impact history, this research also has implications for other craters on other worlds. By counting them and using radiometry to estimate their ages, researchers can estimate when there were major swarms of asteroids impacting the inner solar system. In turn, that supplies potential evidence for the path the giant planets took during their early orbital history, feeding into a theory known as the Nice model.

But weâre not done with the lunar landscape yet. The SPA is a prime target for future crewed missions, and as more rovers, landers, and, potentially, people start to traverse the wilds of the lunar surface, theyâll occasionally come across fragments of the ancient crust created by massive impacts beyond anything our species has ever witnessed in the solar system. Itâs kind of cool to think that those fragments have been waiting billions of years for us to find and study them.

2026 Was the Year Restaurants Went Full Midwest

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (926 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eater

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s a giardinera- and tavern-style-stuffed, totally welcoming time in hospitality.
  • At Kyle Knall’s Milwaukee restaurant Cassis, the showstopper dish is ravioli Dauphiné, a sheet of 24 tiny squares stuffed with the Wisconsin cheese Pleasant Ridge Reserve.
  • The Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, feature serious Midwest representation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s a giardinera- and tavern-style-stuffed, totally welcoming time in hospitality.

At Kyle Knall’s Milwaukee restaurant Cassis, the showstopper dish is ravioli Dauphiné, a sheet of 24 tiny squares stuffed with the Wisconsin cheese Pleasant Ridge Reserve. Topped with glazed seasonal veggies, kernels of sweet corn in summer and sliced honeynut squash in late fall, it speaks to Knall’s Midwestern-meets-French approach—one of the reasons why his restaurant earned a slot on Eater’s 2026 list of the Best New Restaurants in America.

The Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, feature serious Midwest representation. The Best Fresh Restaurants list includes Chicago’s Creepies, which also digs into that Midwest-French mashup, and Kansas City’s Akoya Omakase, which brings a distinct viewpoint to the omakase experience. Meanwhile, the pickled walleye cheeks at Rosy in Cleveland and the puffed grain toast at All Well in Chicago are among the Restaurant Dishes of the Year, and Chicago’s Bad Butter, a place best-known for its croissant take on a Chicago-style hot dog, is one of the Best New Bakeries. It even includes drinks—Culebra, a Puerto Rican spot that draws on the Latinx influences of its Chicago neighborhood, is on Punch’s Best New Bars list. Between these accolades and other national recognition, all eyes are on the Midwest right now. And that’s even before we get into the impact of the Chicago-set show The Bear, which put Italian beef on everyone’s radar, and the rise of tavern-style pizza around the country.

The Midwest has always had great restaurants, of course, but it’s undeniable that something has shifted. “People are flying into these cities rather than flying over them,” states Vinnie Cimino, the Cleveland chef who co-owns Rosy and Cordelia. “I think that word is getting out about these smaller pockets of culture and cuisine.” Some of this is attributable to diners being more willing to explore outside major coastal cities, but it’s also due to chefs returning home to the region. “Post-pandemic, a lot of folks moved out of larger cities and back home,” says Cimino. “Now they’re setting up shop and creating great things in the spaces that they grew up in.” David Posey, chef and co-owner of Creepies and Elske in Chicago, agrees, adding: “For a long time, it felt like we were playing catch-up with trends on the coasts. Now I think we’re less quick to follow trends and are more confident in having our own voice of what the Midwest is.”.

One of those chefs who left Newly introduced York is Knall, a Birmingham, Alabama, native who cooked at Gramercy Tavern in New York before moving to his wife’s hometown of Milwaukee in 2020. Another is Peter Hoang, who worked at his father’s Kansas City, Missouri, sushi restaurant before gaining experience in Chicago and New York restaurants. When he returned to open Akoya Omakase, he crafted menus with the audience in mind, with two omakases, priced more affordably than many at $85 and $165, as well as an à la carte menu. “My sushi is honed by Japanese techniques and sourcing,” he states. “But I interpret what I think is best for the fish, whether that’s highlighting the textures and flavors through different garnishes or using aging or salting techniques.”.

It’s not simply that these are good restaurants located in the Midwest—these restaurants are deeply Midwestern in ethos. In Chicago, David and Anna Posey, who run the Michelin-starred Elske, wanted to open a French bistro for their second venture. But as they developed Creepies with chef de cuisine Tayler Ploshehanski, David Posey says they began expanding its focus: “We started taking flavors and adapting them to things that we’re a little more familiar with.” This means dishes that draw on the traditions of Michigan, Wisconsin, and Illinois—think tarte flambée on a tavern-style pizza crust and mussels with giardiniera. And it’s not just the food at Creepies that reflects the Midwest: “We told our designer that our inspiration board was a Midwest basement with wood paneling and low ceilings meets a bistro in the French countryside.”.

In a recent development, at Cordelia, Cimino leans into the traditional cuisine of Northeast Ohio, with offerings like raw-beef cannibal sandwiches and kielbasa with cabbage salad. “It’s the familiar flavors that we grew up eating, rethought into this more modern light,” he says. Meanwhile, Rosy “is a deeper dive into the culture of our region” and features dishes like Balkan cevapi and Italian cotechino cooked over live fire. The approach is drawing a wide range of Cleveland diners, from 20-somethings there for the cool, candlelit vibe to grandparents there to taste the food they grew up with. “I think that’s what the Midwest is,” Cimino says. “Being able to be that transgenerational space everybody feels welcome in.”.

Industry observers note that that welcoming community sensibility is a key component of Midwestern restaurants. Knall counts several farmers and shoppers at the West Allis Farmers Market, where he sources for Cassis, as some of his regulars. “To me, it indicates that’s really what Midwest food is: supporting those communities,” he says.

Perhaps more than anything, it’s hospitality that sets these spots apart. “Hospitality is our biggest focus between both restaurants and maybe even more of a focus than the food,” Knall claims. “To me, the way that our team makes you feel in the restaurants is such a Midwest thing.” And at Cordelia, where the slogan is “Midwest Nice,” Cimino says: “It’s welcoming you into our proverbial home.”.

Security Footage Catches Two Zoo Gorillas Forming a “Living Ladder” To Outsmart an Electric Fence

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (935 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two zoo gorillas repeatedly teamed up for food despite rarely spending time together, showing that a shared effort does not always end with a shared meal.
  • A leafy branch was out of reach for two gorillas at the Ramat Gan Safari, and an electric barrier around the trunk blocked a direct climb.
  • In a recent development, the most extensively documented event came to light in September 2024, when keepers noticed the pair peacefully eating bark and leaves from a large branch that had previously been beyond their reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two zoo gorillas repeatedly teamed up for food despite rarely spending time together, showing that a shared effort does not always end with a shared meal.

A leafy branch was out of reach for two gorillas at the Ramat Gan Safari, and an electric barrier around the trunk blocked a direct climb. The female western lowland gorillas, half-sisters Amelia and Lisha, formed a “living ladder,” with Lisha providing a steady back for Amelia to stand on.

In a recent development, the most extensively documented event came to light in September 2024, when keepers noticed the pair peacefully eating bark and leaves from a large branch that had previously been beyond their reach. Staff reviewed security camera footage to find out how they had obtained it.

According to recent reports, the recording highlighted Amelia walking over and climbing onto a rock beneath a Peltophorum dubium tree. Lisha joined her and stood firmly on all fours on the rock. Amelia then climbed onto Lisha’s back, stood upright, and reached up to grasp and break off a branch approximately 4.5 meters, or 15 feet, above the ground. The rock, Lisha’s stable posture, and Amelia’s reach together made the branch accessible.

Researchers documented three events involving the same pair in 2021, 2024, and 2025, with each gorilla performing the same role every time. Neither had been trained to perform the maneuver. The team describes their behavior as a rare example of spontaneous cooperation between adult gorillas, with a clear division of roles.

In a recent development, published in Primates, the study was led by Michael Levitzky and Prof. Israel Hershkovitz of the Department of Anatomy and Anthropology at the Gray Faculty of Medical and Health Sciences and the Dan David Center for Human Evolution and Biohistory Research at Tel Aviv University.

Yehonatan Samocha, Head of the Primate Section at the Ramat Gan Safari (Zoological Center Tel Aviv-Ramat Gan), said, “At the Ramat Gan Safari we have observed and studied animal behaviors for years, closely following their relationships, social bonds, and fascinating capabilities. Particularly among great apes, including gorillas, we repeatedly encounter behaviors that demonstrate high intelligence, learning ability, problem-solving, complex communication, and cooperation.

“This is why we are so thrilled, though not necessarily surprised, by the cooperation between Amelia and Lisha. We are familiar with their abilities and understand how intelligent and curious they are, and how capable they are of learning from one another and working together. Sometimes, our surprise tells us more about our expectations of animals than their actual abilities. The study’s great importance lies in providing scientific documentation and analysis for observations and behaviors we encounter in our daily work, allowing us to enhance our knowledge of gorillas, their social world, and their cognitive abilities.”.

In a recent development, in the June 2025 footage, Lisha positioned herself with her back toward Amelia, who was not observed using force. Levitzky, who initiated and led the study, explained how the recording helped the researchers interpret Lisha’s participation.

In a recent development, “When I first watched the footage, it was clear to me that this was something extraordinary. What I find fascinating is that Leisha did more than simply serve as a ‘step’ for Amelia. She appeared to participate actively and willingly in solving the problem, approaching on her own initiative and positioning herself in exactly the right place, without Amelia physically guiding her. This is the difference between using another individual as a tool and true cooperation, in which both individuals work together toward the same goal.

“For years, gorillas were considered less cognitively sophisticated than other great apes. As more observations like these accumulate, we will be able to deepen and refine our understanding of their social and cognitive abilities. Future studies involving systematic documentation and audio recordings could help us decipher how they coordinate with one another, and perhaps also teach us something about the roots of cooperation in our own species.”.

Sources indicate that the sisters generally spend little time together, sleep in separate night quarters, and rarely groom one another. Their teamwork also had different outcomes at feeding time. Although keepers reported peaceful sharing after the 2024 event, Amelia alone ate the vegetation in the observed 2025 sequence, showing that cooperating to obtain food did not necessarily lead to sharing it.

Industry observers note that hershkovitz remarked, “Our observations reveal how two gorillas can join forces and assume complementary roles to solve a problem that neither can solve on her own. It is particularly intriguing that this cooperation recurs even though the two do not usually display much closeness, and even when the food is not shared between them afterward. These observations are important for understanding human evolution because they offer an explanation, albeit a partial one, for how we survived on the savanna – through social support and a high level of cooperation that can occur even without language or preplanning. Although the number of observations is small, they offer a window into gorillas’ ability to learn from experience, coordinate their actions, and draw on one another and their surroundings to achieve a shared goal.”.

Recent findings suggest that the study involved only two gorillas and three documented events. The available footage could not establish whether they communicated through vocalizations or subtle gestures, or whether they planned their actions in advance.

Recent findings suggest that reference: “Cooperation in adult female western lowland gorillas: complex problem-solving through learned spatial affordances and mutual agency” by Michael Levitzky, and Israel Hershkovitz, 24 October 2026, Primates. DOI: 10.1007/s10329-026-01297-6.

Robots, Not Astronauts, Will Have to Fix Space Data Centers

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1277 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yesterday we explored some of the difficulties facing orbital data centers in our look at the bottleneck of launching enough solar panels and radiative cooling systems to power the AI computing boom in space.
  • According to recent reports, modern hardware powering Artificial Intelligence even on Earth has an obsolescence problem.
  • Unfortunately, that means throwing away literal tons of still-useful solar panels and heat radiators just to discard some obsolete computer hardware.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yesterday we explored some of the difficulties facing orbital data centers in our look at the bottleneck of launching enough solar panels and radiative cooling systems to power the AI computing boom in space. JPL physicist Dr. Slava Turyshev, who wrote the paper at the center of that article, also published a follow-up study in August, available in preprint on arXiv, about how getting the hardware off the ground is only half the battle. Once all that equipment is up there, someone, or something, is going to have to maintain it.

According to recent reports, modern hardware powering Artificial Intelligence even on Earth has an obsolescence problem. The computer chips and memory that power AI data centers become obsolete every 3-5 years. If a manufacturer builds an orbital data center, its processing power is effectively useless for training the latest AI models in less than half a decade. So, in their business aims, the solution is to build intentionally disposable satellites.

Unfortunately, that means throwing away literal tons of still-useful solar panels and heat radiators just to discard some obsolete computer hardware. Given that those bulkier pieces of equipment pose their own challenge for debuts, as we saw yesterday, that seems a bit of a waste. So, Dr. Turyshev suggests that orbital data centers must be designed with hardware replacement in mind.

Fraser talks about a NASA project designed to assemble large-scale structures in space.

Industry observers note that on Earth, replacement of data server racks involves a human technician walking down an air-conditioned aisle, pulling some cables, and pressing pins before replacing a standardized blade. In orbit, that would require a pressurized housing with airlocks, life support and fire suppression systems, while still having the problem of cooling all of those heat-producing microchips in the vacuum of space. According to Dr. Turyshev, that means the entire data center architecture should be based around plug-and-play âorbital replacement unitsâ (ORUs).

He assigns each of those ORUs into one of three main replaceable component tiers (alongside replacing an entire 100 kW satellite node if it suffers catastrophic damage). One is a 5 kW âcomputeâ module that holds the memory, storage and optical transceivers necessary to actually perform calculations. These are designed to be rapidly swappable, and are intended to be the most replaced part of the whole satellite.

According to recent reports, another ORU category is the âsubsystemsâ â the power converters, batteries, pumps, and manifolds meant to keep the whole system running but that are settled enough technologically to not require regular replacement. In the paperâs architecture, these can be swapped out by specialized 6 or 7 degree-of-freedom robotic arms, as compared to the automated cartridge changers that handle replacing the compute modules.

Fraser talks about the difficulties repairing missions at L2, like JWST.

The third group of ORUs consists of the solar arrays and radiator panels themselves. Making them modular has the added advantage of not needing to replace the entire cooling or power generation system if one part happens to be struck by a micrometeoroid, which will undoubtedly happen often even in Low Earth Orbit. Despite the fact these modules make up the bulk of the weight and surface area of the spacecraft, they will not have to be repaired as frequently as the compute modules, as random failures caused by cosmic rays will brick compute modules fairly frequently..

Unfortunately, replacing these systems isnât as easy as it would be on Earth. Each 5 kW processor will heat up nearly half a degree Celsius every second, triggering a thermal overload in a little less than a minute if left uncooled. And the power capacitors riding along to maintain power to the system have the capability of producing an arc strong enough to weld a robotic gripper to a maintenance touch point, so they must be bled off before a robot can start interacting with the satelliteâs hardware.

Sources indicate that and then, there is once again the sense of scale. For a standardized 1 MW cluster, comprising ten 100 kW sized systems, a collection of 3-4 robots specialized assigned to each 1MW cluster would have to perform around four hundred standardized swaps per year â more than one a day. This would include replacing broken or damaged parts, as well as upgrading to the server hardware itself.

It has been revealed that hubble has already been repaired by a crewed mission. NASA wants to do it again, Great Space expliains. Credit - Great Space YouTube Channel.

Recent findings suggest that scaling that up once again to a 1 GW computer cluster, comparable to a major modern AI campus here on Earth, the number becomes staggering. There would have to be 400,000 automated replacement tasks every year. And supplying the parts to do that would require launching up to 25 metric tons of replacement cargo every day.

According to recent reports, to put it bluntly, we donât have that kind of launch capacity yet. Nor would sending humans up help manage such a drastic workload. The paper estimates that housing and feeding a crew of 4-6 technicians to actively manage a data center constellation would require $500 million to $1.5 billion per year. Until we get to the scale of several hundred megawatts to a gigawatt-level system, that is not economically feasible.

According to recent reports, thatâs not to say we couldnât launch specialized crewed repair missions occasionally. But at the scales needed to make a dent in the AI infrastructure we have down here on Earth, it would be hard to keep up with the overall maintenance workload using humans. And unfortunately, the entire concept of maintenance is another area that the back-of-the-envelope calculations of the companies that want to build orbital data centers seem to ignore.

In a recent development, their solution is simply to add some extra hardware to account for the inevitable damage/failure that comes with operating in space. While that might work for a little while, if the plan is to have a long-term data center presence in orbit, it's better to design for at least the possibility of continual operation rather than burning up tens of thousands of satellites in fireballs across the world every year. It remains to be seen if that message will get across to the people designing these systems, though.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Frame TVs are one of the more interesting home theater innovations in recent years, mostly because they prioritize “form” as much as “function.” They take a two-pronged approach: offering high-definition 4K entertainment and decor in one fell swoop.

America’s Data Centers Have a Hidden Death Toll, MIT Researchers Warn

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An MIT analysis estimates that powering America’s data centers contributed to hundreds of premature deaths in a single year, with rural populations facing greater risks than city dwellers.
  • Recent findings suggest that as artificial intelligence drives the rapid construction of data centers across the United States, concerns about their environmental impact are taking on a new dimension.
  • In a recent development, researchers at MIT estimate that air pollution associated with data center electricity consumption contributed to approximately 650 premature deaths in the United States in 2023 alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An MIT analysis estimates that powering America’s data centers contributed to hundreds of premature deaths in a single year, with rural populations facing greater risks than city dwellers.

Recent findings suggest that as artificial intelligence drives the rapid construction of data centers across the United States, concerns about their environmental impact are taking on a new dimension. The electricity needed to keep these facilities running around the clock can increase air pollution in communities far from where the data centers themselves are built, potentially putting the health of people who live nowhere near them at risk.

In a recent development, researchers at MIT estimate that air pollution associated with data center electricity consumption contributed to approximately 650 premature deaths in the United States in 2023 alone. Iowa, Nevada, South Dakota, and Kansas had the highest estimated rates of premature deaths per capita, even though much of the electricity demand was concentrated in northern Virginia and Texas. Rates in Virginia and Texas were only about half those in most Midwestern states.

“When people think about the negative impacts of data centers, they usually focus on the neighbors. But our study indicates that the air quality impacts of data centers are very widespread across a large region. Even if you don’t think you are affected because there is not a data center near you, think again,” says Noelle Selin, senior author of the study, a professor in the MIT Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS) and the Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences (EAPS), and director of the Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy.

Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated that data centers’ electricity needs accounted for about 4 percent of total U.S. energy demand in 2023 and approximately 4.4 percent of the nation’s overall emissions. Those proportions have likely grown as more facilities have been built.

In a recent development, determining who bears the health consequences of that growing demand is complicated by the interconnected nature of the nation’s power grid. A data center in Virginia, for example, may increase electricity production at power plants in the Ohio Valley, where a greater proportion of older coal and natural gas plants produce higher levels of emissions.

Sources indicate that “Different regions have different mixes of power. If you turn on a major newly introduced demand source, by plugging a data center into the grid, you might have to fire up your really dirty power plant to meet that new demand,” Selin says.

Sources indicate that the pollution can then travel into neighboring states, where local atmospheric conditions can make matters worse. In agricultural regions such as Iowa and Nebraska, ammonia released from fertilizer promotes the formation of fine particulate matter (PM2.5), microscopic airborne particles that can cause heart attacks, strokes, and lung disease.

Recent findings suggest that the estimated health consequences also extend to Kansas, South Dakota, Missouri, and Arkansas. Overall, the researchers found that rural populations face a significantly higher estimated mortality risk from data center electricity demand than urban populations.

It has been revealed that to understand how these risks are distributed, the team developed a model that tracks electricity production and transmission between regions on an hourly basis. While many previous studies relied on average power grid emissions, the researchers assumed that data centers operated around the clock and identified which individual generators would respond to their additional electricity needs.

“Generators that respond to additional electricity demand are often natural gas plants, although the response varies by place and hour,” says Yuang (Albert) Chen, an MIT graduate student and co-author of the study.

Industry observers note that “It was a challenge to gather all the data,” Chen says. “There are more than 10,000 generators in the U.S. grid, and we needed to make sure the data provided for each generator is valid and validated across other data sources.”.

It has been revealed that the researchers calculated emissions of nitrogen oxides and sulfur dioxide from individual generators. Both pollutants contribute to the formation of fine particulate matter, while nitrogen oxides also help produce ground-level ozone, commonly associated with smog.

Using a separate atmospheric model, the team simulated how these pollutants formed and traveled across regions. They then drew on epidemiological research linking air pollution to premature death to estimate the resulting health impacts.

In a recent development, of the approximately 650 premature deaths estimated for 2023, 513 were attributed to fine particulate matter and 137 to smog. Together, they represented about 5.3 percent of all estimated electricity-related premature deaths nationwide.

“While it is not surprising that any additional source of air pollution will result in mortalities, with data centers, when and where these deaths are occurring are different than you might expect,” Selin notes.

As companies continue to expand their computing infrastructure, the findings suggest that decisions about where to build data centers and how to power them need to account for public health well beyond the immediate surroundings.

Industry observers note that “When people are thinking about data center siting and operations, it is notable to consider more than just things like land and energy prices. They should also take air quality considerations into the equation,” Chen says. “This is a good baseline to think about where we should build data centers and how we should supply those data centers with electricity.”.

Sources indicate that the researchers hope to investigate the air quality consequences of a growing industry trend in which data centers incorporate their own on-site power plants. They could also examine whether adjusting when these facilities consume electricity could reduce their impact on air quality.

Industry observers note that reference: “Spatially distributed air quality and health impacts of data center electricity demand in the United States” by Yuang Chen, Shen Wang, Juan Ramon L Senga, Andrew Scott White, Anthony YH Wong, Lyssa M Freese, Michelle L Bell and Noelle E Selin, 19 November 2026, Environmental Research Letters. DOI: 10.1088/1748-9326/aebbd4.

This research was funded, in part, by the MIT Energy Initiative Society of Energy Scholars and the MIT Martin Family Society of Fellows for Sustainability.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that astronomers have detected titanium oxide in gas form for the first time around a young, massive star. The detection offers a rare glimpse into the very earliest stages of solar system formation, before the formation of planets and asteroids.

The detection was made around a young protostar called Orion Source I, which lies some 1500 light-years from Earth. Orion Source I has not yet reached the main sequence phase of a starâs life cycle â it continues to accrete material from its surrounding molecular cloud.

Models of solar system formation have long held that certain rocky molecules, ones which are stable at high temperatures, act as the âseedsâ that make up the dust in a protoplanetary disk, and later form the basis for rocky planets like Earth and Mars. This includes elements like calcium, aluminum, and titanium. Only later do materials that vaporize easily â volatiles like water, for example â accrete to young solar system objects.

Sources indicate that but itâs not exactly clear where these seeds form. Samples collected from our own solar system suggest that they form under high-temperature conditions. They are, as far as we can tell, the oldest solids ever formed in our solar system.

Now, for the first time, this detection of titanium oxide around Orion Source I is providing astronomers more direct evidence of vaporized rock at the dawn of a new star system.

âWe're in a unique situation with this object, Orion Source I,â mentioned Adam Ginsburg, Associate Professor at the University of Florida and a co-author on the paper announcing the discovery. âThis object has a luminous enough star that it's evaporating the rock. We're seeing the rock evaporate from solid into gas, and so we can do the spectroscopy now and figure out what the rock is made of.â.

Ginsberg and his coauthors are getting the first real glimpses at the formation environments of these rocky dust-seeding materials, which complements knowledge gathered from our own solar system.

Sources indicate that âThe exciting thing is we're seeing the titanium oxide; we can measure how much there is, and we can start comparing our measurements to how our own solar system formed,â Ginsburg remarked. âIn our solar system, we can measure the ratios between different types of rocks, different elements, because we can grab those rocks and bring them into a lab.â.

Sources indicate that this isnât the first time Orion Source I has provided valuable insights into solar system formation. In 2019, salty compounds were similarly detected in the protoplanetary disk.

While the salt was found mainly in the outer disk around the star, the titanium oxide was found closer in, at the base of the starâs outflow of material: a hotter, more extreme region where the material could be vaporized. Understanding the origin of this material is an crucial discovery for researchers trying to piece together exactly how a new solar system comes together, and offers a glimpse into the past of our own star and rocky neighbourhood.

The detection was published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters in 2026.

Earth’s Lakes Are Changing in Unison – and Scientists Are Worried

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (645 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lakes play an crucial role in regulating Earth’s carbon cycle, and scientists warn that environmental changes occurring across many lakes at once could amplify global climate risks.
  • Industry observers note that lakes around the world are increasingly changing in step, a trend that could weaken a natural buffer against environmental disruption.
  • The characteristics of a lake’s watershed, the land that drains into it, have historically helped buffer its ecosystem against broader environmental changes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lakes play an crucial role in regulating Earth’s carbon cycle, and scientists warn that environmental changes occurring across many lakes at once could amplify global climate risks.

Industry observers note that lakes around the world are increasingly changing in step, a trend that could weaken a natural buffer against environmental disruption. A new study found that this synchronization has accelerated markedly since 2000.

The characteristics of a lake’s watershed, the land that drains into it, have historically helped buffer its ecosystem against broader environmental changes. Lakes fluctuated independently, a pattern known as “spatial asynchrony” that spread ecological disturbances across time and space.

According to recent reports, A team led by Prof. Ke Zhang of the Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (NIGLAS) combined century-scale sediment records with continuous satellite observations from approximately 2,000 lakes. Alongside growing synchrony, the researchers found a significant decline in network modularity, meaning the lake network was becoming less divided into groups with distinct patterns of change.

The researchers used water clarity and phytoplankton biomass, the mass of microscopic organisms that use sunlight to make food, as proxies for lake metabolic activity. These indicators provide an indirect view of how lake ecosystems process energy and nutrients. Their growing synchrony suggests that the underlying carbon, nutrient, and biodiversity dynamics they reflect may also be becoming more synchronized.

The study attributes this shift to environmental telecoupling, connections through which climate extremes such as heatwaves and socioeconomic pressures link changes across distant regions. The authors describe this increasingly linked response to large-scale environmental change as a new hallmark of the Anthropocene, a term used to describe a world profoundly shaped by human activity.

Sources indicate that although lakes cover less than 2% of Earth’s surface, they help regulate global carbon and nutrient cycles and biodiversity. Losing the differences in how they respond to environmental pressures could therefore have consequences well beyond individual watersheds.

“This loss of buffering capacity transforms lakes from passive, regionally distinct systems into active amplifiers of global environmental risks. Synchronized lakes can concentrate biophysical fluxes, potentially triggering high-amplitude global pulses, such as simultaneous greenhouse gas emissions or widespread aquatic hypoxia, thereby exacerbating the triple planetary crisis,” Zhang said.

In a recent development, aquatic hypoxia means a shortage of oxygen in the water. The “triple planetary crisis” refers to climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution.

It has been revealed that water management has traditionally treated lakes as isolated local resources, creating what the researchers describe as a “scale mismatch” between governance and the processes shaping these ecosystems. Zhang and his co-authors propose treating interconnected lake networks as a dynamically coupled “Planetary Commons.” Their objective is to protect the local ecological processes that maintain variation across landscapes, without seeking to eliminate synchrony.

Recent findings suggest that to put that idea into practice, the team introduced a framework called Strategic Planetary Lake Areas (SPLAs). By tracking large-scale measures of synchrony and modularity, policymakers could identify priority regions, including regional groups of lakes whose behavior is rapidly converging. These areas could become candidates for targeted polycentric governance, an approach involving multiple centers of decision-making.

“This research not only redefines the critical importance of inland waters in global change studies but also introduces a macroscale dimension to international sustainable development agendas,” Zhang said. “The work emphasizes that preserving the diversity of ecological responses is essential for maintaining long-term Earth-system stability in an increasingly interconnected world.”.

Recent findings suggest that reference: “Global lake synchrony signals rising planetary-scale ecological coupling” by Ke Zhang, Yaoyao Han, Lindsey Gillson, Xiaoling Zhang, Suzanne McGowan, Michael E.
