A Train Carrying Deadly Materials Was on Fire for Nearly an Hour as It Barreled Toward a Small Town. Why Didn’t Anyone Stop It?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3590 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Editor’s note: In July 2024, after this story was published, the National Transportation Safety Board released its final analysis on the Norfolk Southern freight train derailment in East Palestine, Ohio.
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • In a recent development, on the frigid evening of Friday, February 3, 2023, at around 8:50 p.m., a Norfolk Southern freight train measuring more than a mile and three quarters long snaked its way through the town of East Palestine, Ohio.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s note: In July 2024, after this story was published, the National Transportation Safety Board released its final analysis on the Norfolk Southern freight train derailment in East Palestine, Ohio. It also released a companion illustrated digest of the incident. The analysis determined that the train derailed after an overheated wheel bearing caused an axel to “burn off.” The punctured DOT-111 tank car leaked butyl acrylates, which are flammable and likely started the post-derailment fires. Further, the decision to intentionally “vent and burn” vinyl chloride tank cars was likely unnecessary and based on incomplete or misleading information, according to the report. The NTSB issued 34 newly introduced safety recommendations covering several needs, including defect detection systems, tank car standards, hazardous materials, and emergency response procedures.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

In a recent development, on the frigid evening of Friday, February 3, 2023, at around 8:50 p.m., a Norfolk Southern freight train measuring more than a mile and three quarters long snaked its way through the town of East Palestine, Ohio. The train consisted of 149 cars, pulled by three locomotives—two at the front, one in the middle—and traveled just under 50 miles per hour. Of those 149 cars, 20 were tankers labeled with hazardous-materials placards. Several of the tankers contained liquefied vinyl chloride gas, the combustible and carcinogenic precursor material for PVC pipe; others contained ethylene glycol, a toxic ingredient in antifreeze. Driving the lead locomotive was Tony Faison, the train’s engineer; with him were the train’s conductor and a trainee.

According to recent reports, engineers chart their progress by designated mile markers along the track. About 20 minutes earlier, the train had crossed mile marker 69.0, just east of Salem, Ohio. While crossing that spot, an infrared sensor built into the track called a “hotbox detector” had reported elevated temperatures on one of the front axles of the 23rd railcar. The ambient temperature that night was 10 degrees Fahrenheit. The bearings on the axle had reached an abnormally hot temperature of 103. The car, a hopper designed to hold commodities like grain, wasn’t carrying hazardous materials, but the hotbox detector relayed an alert to Norfolk Southern’s Atlanta command center all the same. No further action was taken.

According to recent reports, as the train left East Palestine, it approached Ohio’s border with Pennsylvania, passing within a few hundred feet of the State Line Tavern, a local watering hole. There, at 8:55 p.m., it crossed mile marker 49.8. As the twenty-third car crossed the next hotbox detector, the infrared sensors revealed that the temperature of the axle’s bearings had risen sharply, to over 250 degrees. Faison immediately received an audio message from the locomotive’s onboard computer to stop the train. He reacted quickly to apply the brakes, but it was too late. He didn’t know it, but for the previous 40 minutes, his train had been on fire.

Industry observers note that the train took more than a thousand feet to come to a stop. As it did, the compromised axle gave way. The left-side journal box, which held the axle in place, broke off and landed on one side of the track; the wheelset, consisting of the axle with two steel wheels mounted at both ends, ended up on the other. The twenty-third car jumped the rail, and the cars behind it followed suit, creating a tremendous series of crashes that could be heard throughout town. Thirty-eight railcars piled up, including 11 of the hazmat tankers.

In a recent development, faison leaped from the locomotive to inspect the damage. From his standpoint at the front of the train, he could see flames rising into the night. He immediately contacted 911. So did many of the town’s residents, reporting both the train crash and the fire. One thought a gas station had exploded.

According to recent reports, in the next few hours, the toxic flames would force an evacuation of the town. The specter of chemical poisoning lingered over East Palestine for months. And even today, the question of how a system of detectors—expressly designed to prevent this kind of derailment—failed to notice a dangerously overheated train axle remains unanswered.

Sources indicate that in the minutes after the derailment, first responders rushed to the blaze, but they were initially underequipped. Serving a town of fewer than five thousand people, the East Palestine fire department was a mostly volunteer force. The sole professional on staff was Chief Keith Drabick, who on that night was almost three hundred miles away, driving through Pennsylvania on vacation. Informed of the crash at 9 p.m., Drabick turned his car around and drove straight back to East Palestine, but he didn’t arrive until five hours later. For the first few minutes, volunteers had to fight the blaze alone. Meanwhile, following protocol, Faison cut the first two locomotives from the train and moved them a mile down the track. In the confusion that followed, some firefighters seemed unaware they were responding to a hazmat site and reported to residents that the burning train cars were carrying only malt liquor.

According to recent reports, some of the train cars were carrying malt liquor, but others contained stronger stuff. As the scope of the disaster slowly became clear, the volunteers were joined by professional firefighting crews from nearby counties, including a special hazmat squad. At 9:45 p.m., concerned about the risks of a vinyl chloride explosion as well as the toxic cocktail of flaming chemicals escaping into the night, officials began evacuating nearby homes. Meanwhile, some of the contents of the leaking tankers began seeping into nearby Sulphur Run, a stream that flowed directly from the crash site through the center of town.

According to recent reports, even before the official order, citizens had started to evacuate. East Palestine resident Jami Wallace had learned of the train wreck from her mother. Wallace, a human resources manager in her forties, had recently gotten engaged. She called her fiancé, who was with a friend at the State Line Tavern. Driving past the burning crash site, he raced home to collect Wallace and their three-year-old daughter. “Grabbed her a couple of changes of clothes and out the door we went,” she told me. “We didn’t even know where we were going. It was the middle of winter and the heater was broken in the car.”.

After an hour and a half of firefighting, the Ohio State Police expanded the evacuation zone to one mile surrounding the derailment site. Around midnight, still fearing an explosion, the firefighters retreated. They then began to survey the crash site with aerial drones, in an attempt to determine which specific chemicals were leaking. The survey was challenging: The site was, well, a train wreck, and some of the plastic hazardous-materials placards had melted in the fire.

Eventually, responders determined that three hazmat cars had been physically breached. One contained ethylene glycol, the antifreeze ingredient, which can be lethal in concentrated doses. The other two contained acrylates, used as base ingredients in adhesives and paint. All three materials were burning off, releasing volatile organic compounds into the air. The fire was additionally fueled by nonhazardous but flammable railcar cargo, including several tankers loaded with petroleum lubricants. For days to come, an ominous toxic cloud hung suspended over the site. “You know how smoke, like, moves through the sky? Yeah, this wasn’t moving anywhere,” Wallace said. “It was almost like a green cloud that was, like, hovering.”.

Initially, none of the vinyl chloride tankers were breached. (If they had been, a series of explosions might have occurred, and the cancer-causing chemical could have rained down on the town.) Still, five vinyl chloride tankers, containing more than 115,000 gallons of vinyl chloride in total, had piled up in the burn zone. Each tanker had an emergency pressure release valve designed to vent gas into the atmosphere. Over the next few days, as temperatures rose inside the tanks, these valves automatically opened and closed, periodically releasing excess vinyl chloride gas into the air—where it immediately caught fire. In one extraordinary display on the evening of Saturday, February 4, one of the tanker valves vented for 70 continuous minutes, creating a spectacular flamethrower.

With the crash site cordoned off and the tankers burping flames, officials deliberated on what to do. One worry was that the release valves on the tankers were starting to suffer thermal damage. Another was that the vinyl chloride inside the tanks might “polymerize,” forming into chains of PVC, which might cause the valves to stick, sealing the pressure in and causing the tankers to blow.

From the outside, the hazmat experts couldn’t be sure if polymerization was occurring. Eventually they settled on two options. One option was to deliberately puncture the tanks and conduct a controlled burn of the vinyl chloride gas. The other option was to wait it out and hope the tanks cooled down enough so they wouldn’t explode. Chief Drabick was presented with this devil’s bargain: Wait, and potentially watch the exploding tanks rain shrapnel and poisonous chemicals on his town, or release mass quantities of vinyl chloride—a known Group A carcinogen—into the atmosphere. “I was given 13 minutes to make a decision,” Drabick told investigators from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), the federal agency responsible for investigating the wreck.

After consulting with his chief officers, Drabick chose to vent and burn. Following an expanded evacuation order, specialists attached explosive charges to the exteriors of five damaged tanker cars. At 4:37 p.m. on February 6, the charges were detonated, sending twin columns of flaming vinyl chloride gas high into the air and obscuring the setting sun with thick, black smoke. The burn continued through the following day; it was not until February 8, five days after the axle on train car 23 had first started to burn, that the fire was fully put out.

East Palestine soon found itself host to another kind of toxic cocktail, one consisting of corporate communications specialists, blustering public officials, government bureaucrats, and enterprising class-action attorneys. Complementing this splendid company were the more respectable representatives of the NTSB. Leading the agency’s efforts was Ruben Payan, an NTSB veteran with a heavy build, a thick mustache, and a calm and measured voice. Under his patient command, the NTSB began a thorough investigation of the crash site and the events leading up to the derailment.

According to recent reports, the agency published the first investigation update to its website in March 2023. And then on June 22, Payan presented his preliminary results at a public meeting in East Palestine. (It was the first onsite NTSB meeting in six years.) Using security camera footage collected from homes and businesses adjacent to the tracks, Payan was able to present a detailed videography of the train’s final minutes. Between the towns of Sebring and East Palestine, more than a dozen surveillance cameras had captured the train in motion; in ten of those camera feeds, the train was plainly on fire. In true-color camera feeds, the lower axle of the twenty-third car glowed a dull orange color; in infrared camera feeds, it blazed an intense white, throwing visible sparks.

In a recent development, the first two cameras to show the fire were in Salem, Ohio, some 26 miles west of East Palestine. The train passed the first camera at 8:11 p.m., 44 minutes before the derailment. That camera, which overlooked an alley of snow-covered cars, caught the train in the far background, its axle glowing orange. The camera was located six miles in front of the Salem hotbox detector—the one that had sent an alert to Atlanta but did not stop the train.

How had the Salem hotbox detector missed the fire? The cameras clearly showed flames and sparks along the length of the bottom of the twenty-third car, but when that same car crossed the hotbox detector 10 minutes later, infrared sensors registered the bearing temperatures at only 103 degrees. This wasn’t a case of a sputtering fire that started and stopped, either—the cameras along the route showed a steady blaze. The NTSB declined to comment for this story, citing the pending results of the final investigation. Norfolk Southern declined to comment as well.

I put the question to David Farwick, a veteran engineer who commanded trains in Ohio for Norfolk Southern for nearly 40 years. He told me that Norfolk Southern’s systems were well maintained and up to date. “Those hotbox detectors, they’re pretty sensitive,” he noted. “It’s not like we were working with 1960s stuff. They were pretty good.” The detectors are positioned among the crossties on the track and use infrared sensors to scan the undercarriage of the train. More than 6,000 are deployed across North America. The sensors on the hotbox detectors line up directly with the roller bearings. Farwick seemed flabbergasted that a flaming train had crossed a detector and not tripped an immediate brake alert. “It blows my mind,” he said.

Sources indicate that regulators have also grown concerned in recent years about how long the trains are getting. Farwick told me trains are growing so long that engineers have trouble seeing the backs of them, even on a curve. I asked him whether the train crew would have known they were carrying hazardous materials. “Absolutely,” he said. Farwick explained that the conductor on each train carries a bound paper manifest of the train’s cargo known as a “consist.” In the event of a derailment or crash, a hard copy of this consist is to be immediately delivered to first responders. But Drabick, when questioned by NTSB investigators, said his firefighters never received the consist directly from the Norfolk Southern train crew: “I do not believe that we had any contact with those individuals,” he said. Drabick was only fully informed of the train’s hazardous contents when he arrived on site hours later.

The other looming question about the crash involves the degree of environmental poisoning East Palestine has suffered. In the months following the vent and burn of vinyl chloride gas, Environmental Protection Agency personnel repeatedly visited the town and surrounding areas to take soil samples. Per the EPA’s website, “the sample results indicate that impacts from the smoke and soot were minimal.” The EPA has also monitored the health of the town’s waterways. In the aftermath of the disaster, the agency recorded more than 40,000 dead fish and aquatic animals in the Sulphur Run creek adjacent to the derailment and burn site. While the agency claims that the creek “has not shown any contaminants at levels that exceed health standards since May 1,” it continues to maintain “Keep Out” signs posted around Sulphur Run.

East Palestine is immediately downstream of the crash site, and many local residents believe the creek has delivered poison into their homes. Two days after the derailment, Wallace returned to her evacuated residence to pick up some medication. “As soon as I pulled into my driveway, it hit me in the face—I started coughing ... until, like, I can’t breathe,” she remarked. “I look over because I know it’s the creek. I look over, and I see these chemicals free-floating down.”.

According to recent reports, wallace told me water from the creek regularly seeps into the basement of her residence, and that she has since relocated. She has pushed for the EPA to start indoor monitoring in East Palestine homes; so far, the agency has declined. In any case, the damages Norfolk Southern owes the town are substantial. In June, Norfolk Southern revealed that cleanup costs and injury compensation settlements related to East Palestine would cost the firm nearly $1 billion, though it anticipated that much of that cost would be covered by insurance.

In a statement a couple of weeks after the crash, Jennifer Homendy, the chair of the NTSB, described the accident as “100 percent preventable,” but didn’t offer specifics. She was likely referring to the “hot axle” phenomenon. Train axles use ring-shaped bearings that keep the axle secure while permitting it and the wheels to rotate. A skateboard’s wheels rotate using lubricated ball bearings inside the wheels. Train cars instead use cylindrical roller bearings, which make contact with the axle, permitting easy rotation.

As of December 2023, the NTSB has not yet made a final determination, but multiple experts I talked with told me that they believed a failed roller bearing was the most likely cause of the East Palestine derailment. About two dozen trains derail this way in North America every year. Bearings can fail for any number of reasons, including insufficient lubrication, contamination, overloading, and, simply, age. Once a bearing fails, the axle begins to grind against the metal, and this friction causes a rapid rise in temperature; this was potentially the source of the fire. “Bearings do break down, but that’s the reason why you get these detectors, right?” Farwick said. “That’s exactly what these things are supposed to prevent.”.

Sources indicate that the roller bearings on train axles are sealed inside the wheel and can’t readily be accessed. A faulty one can easily escape visual detection. Hotbox detectors, by using infrared temperature sensors to monitor the bearings in motion, offer a second layer of protection. Generally speaking, they work. Since the early 1980s, train derailments in North America have fallen from more than 7,000 annually to just over 1,000, in part because of hotbox detectors.

Industry observers note that the place to catch the failed roller bearing was not in East Palestine, but 20 miles west, in Salem, Ohio, where the train had crossed a detector 30 minutes before the derailment. That detector had recorded temperatures 93 degrees above the outside environment and sent a noncritical signal to Norfolk Southern central command in Atlanta. Whether dispatchers in Atlanta relayed this warning to the train crew remains unclear; the NTSB has yet to publish transcripts from the train’s black box recorder, and Norfolk Southern has refused to discuss the details of the accident.

Perhaps it is worth noting that in the days before the derailment, the East Palestine train had already been delayed twice by stops for unrelated mechanical issues.

It has been revealed that in March, the NTSB opened a probe into Norfolk Southern’s safety culture. Regulators were concerned not only by the East Palestine derailment, but also two other Ohio derailments in the surrounding months, as well as separate incidents in which three railroad workers on Norfolk Southern lines were killed in a span of 16 months, starting in December of 2021. In a statement announcing the investigation, the NTSB urged Norfolk Southern “to take immediate action today to review and assess its safety practices.”.

This October, Norfolk Southern unveiled a upcoming layer of protection: giant metal sheds, festooned with cameras, that each train will pass through at various points on its journey. The shed is described as a “portal,” and its cameras take an average of 1,000 images per railcar, and send those images to an A.I. data center. Deep-learning algorithms are then employed to spot problems that track detectors and overworked railcar mechanics cannot.

Industry observers note that following the derailment, legislators introduced the bipartisan Railway Safety Act of 2023, which proposed decreasing the required distance between hotbox detectors to 15 miles, from an average of 25 miles today. The legislation is well intended, but it’s not clear if it would have prevented the East Palestine derailment: On that track, the hotbox detectors were an average of 16.7 miles apart. Closing the distance to 15 miles wouldn’t necessarily help.

According to recent reports, the most striking revelation from the NTSB’s preliminary findings was the sheer number of camera feeds that had captured the train car on fire. It costs about $200,000 to install a hotbox detector, and critics have estimated the cost of compliance for the Railway Safety Act at up to $2 billion. Perhaps wireless video cameras could permit dispatchers and AI to regularly monitor the status of the cars, and would give engineers better visibility to the back of the trains.

Finally, there’s still the problem of the toxic derailment site. It remains a hazard zone, and the nearby State Line Tavern remains closed. Under the guidance of the EPA, much of the topsoil near ground zero was excavated. The soil was supposed to be shipped to a hazardous waste facility in Oklahoma, but that state’s governor, Kevin Stitt, blocked the proposal in March. Similarly, the contaminated water from Sulphur Run was drained. The water was supposed to be sent to a treatment facility in Baltimore, but that fell through too.

In a recent development, for a while, the poisoned water and soil remained at the derailment site. “They have these substantial Shamu tanks,” Wallace remarked. “They each hold, like, 100 million gallons of water.” Wallace said a neighbor had flown a drone over the tanks, and seen the chemical sheen on top. Nearby, the toxic dirt was piled into giant mounds, and covered with tarps.

According to recent reports, however, as of January 2026, the EPA reported that personnel had completed a “site-wide cleanup and restoration,” in which crews cleaned the remaining oily sheens from nearby waterways such as Leslie and Sulphur Runs, and removed more than 38 million gallons of wastewater. They also removed any remaining contaminated soil and debris for treatment or disposal, and completed the derailment site excavation. The EPA is now sampling groundwater, surface water, and drinking water quarterly and will continue monitoring the area. Comprehensive updates of the work are available at the EPA’s website.

Paleontologists Discover a Hidden Ecosystem Surrounding a 9.5-Million-Year-Old Whale

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 9.5-million-year-old fossil discovery suggests that an ecological relationship observed in modern oceans has ancient origins.
  • According to recent reports, A whale that sank to the bottom of an ancient sea approximately 9.5 million years ago may have attracted a community of marine scavengers.
  • Named Ophiura huebnerjenseni, the species may provide the earliest fossil evidence of brittle stars gathering around dead whales.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 9.5-million-year-old fossil discovery suggests that an ecological relationship observed in modern oceans has ancient origins.

According to recent reports, A whale that sank to the bottom of an ancient sea approximately 9.5 million years ago may have attracted a community of marine scavengers. Scientists excavating fossil deposits in southern Denmark have discovered microscopic skeletal plates that belong to a previously unknown species of brittle star, a marine invertebrate closely related to starfish.

Named Ophiura huebnerjenseni, the species may provide the earliest fossil evidence of brittle stars gathering around dead whales. Such carcasses create temporary ecosystems known as whale falls, supplying abundant food to organisms living on the seafloor. Brittle stars frequently inhabit these environments today, but their association with whale falls had never been documented in the fossil record.

The remains were recovered from sediment collected during the 2018 excavation of a beaked whale’s lower jaw and several vertebrae at Denmark’s Gram Clay Pit. Researchers washed and sieved the sediment before examining individual microfossils using scanning electron microscopy. Subtle differences in the structure of the brittle stars’ skeletal plates allowed the team to identify a new species.

The distribution of the fossils suggested that their proximity to the whale was more than coincidental.

“Only three samples taken directly beside the whale bones contained brittle-star remains. Samples from the same layer farther from the skeleton, and other comparison samples, yielded none,” the lead author Ben Thuy explains.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers investigated whether ocean currents or favorable fossil preservation conditions could explain the unusual concentration of skeletal plates. Fragments of sea urchins, which have similar physical and chemical properties, provided a useful comparison.

In a recent development, “We considered whether currents had simply concentrated the plates around the bones, or whether local chemical conditions had helped preserve them. However, sea-urchin fragments of comparable size and mineral composition occurred in every sample studied. This makes a preservation-only explanation less likely and supports the interpretation that the brittle stars lived on or close to the whale carcass,” Thuy added.

The Gram Clay Pit preserves sediments deposited beneath the ancient North Sea during the Late Miocene. Although the site has yielded numerous whale skeletons, exceptionally large megalodon vertebrae, and a diverse collection of marine invertebrates, brittle stars had previously escaped detection.

Recent findings suggest that A decomposing whale delivers a substantial supply of organic material to the seabed. In modern oceans, whale falls can support successive communities of scavengers, opportunistic invertebrates, and, particularly in deep water, organisms sustained by chemical processes associated with decomposition.

Although the fossils cannot establish what Ophiura huebnerjenseni ate or whether it depended on whale carcasses, researchers suspect it was a generalist species that normally occupied the surrounding seabed and congregated where food became abundant.

Industry observers note that “We interpret the site as a shallow-water whale fall at a stage when enrichment from the carcass supported opportunistic animals,” said Mette Elstrup. “We found no evidence for the later sulfide-based community stages that can develop at deep-sea whale falls. The discovery therefore adds a rare fossil perspective on how animals responded to a large food source on an ancient shallow-water seabed,” Elstrup said.

Sources indicate that the new species takes its name from Holger Hübner and Thomas Jensen, founders of Germany’s Wacken Open Air heavy metal festival. The connection extends beyond the scientific tribute, however, to the geological origins of the festival’s famously muddy grounds.

Researchers believe the dark gray mud encountered by festivalgoers probably originates from the same geological deposits that preserved the ancient brittle stars.

“The clay that accumulated on the bottom of the ancient North Sea not only preserved the remains of a 9.5-million-years old brittle star, it also turns Wacken Open Air into the muddy battlefield renowned by metalheads worldwide,” concludes Lea Numberger-Thuy.

Reference: “A fresh brittle star (Ophiuroidea, Ophiuridae) associated with a whale fall from the Miocene of Gram, Denmark” by Ben Thuy, Mette Elstrup, Lea D. Numberger-Thuy and Trine Sørensen, 19 October 2026, Neues Jahrbuch für Geologie und Paläontologie – Abhandlungen. DOI: 10.1127/njgpa/2026/1335.

Scientists May Have Finally Found What’s Driving the Universe Apart

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the same fundamental physics that holds atomic nuclei together may also help explain why the Universe is expanding at an accelerating rate.
  • Dark energy accounts for approximately 70 percent of the Universe’s total energy budget, yet its physical origin has remained unknown since scientists discovered cosmic acceleration nearly three decades ago.
  • The proposed explanation centers on Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), the theory describing the strong nuclear force that binds quarks inside protons and neutrons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the same fundamental physics that holds atomic nuclei together may also help explain why the Universe is expanding at an accelerating rate. Researchers at the University of British Columbia (UBC) and the University of Sheffield have developed a theoretical model that connects dark energy to the strong nuclear force, potentially explaining cosmic acceleration without introducing undiscovered particles or newly introduced fundamental fields.

Dark energy accounts for approximately 70 percent of the Universe’s total energy budget, yet its physical origin has remained unknown since scientists discovered cosmic acceleration nearly three decades ago. Many proposed explanations rely on hypothetical particles or fields that have never been detected. The new research, published in The Astrophysical Journal, instead draws on established principles of the Standard Model of particle physics.

The proposed explanation centers on Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), the theory describing the strong nuclear force that binds quarks inside protons and neutrons. According to QCD, even apparently empty space contains quantum fields with complex properties. The researchers suggest that the vacuum’s underlying structure could produce a small energy shift as the Universe expands, potentially accounting for the acceleration observed across cosmic distances.

A key feature of the model involves the vacuum’s topological properties, which describe aspects of its quantum structure that can influence physics over large distances. The researchers propose that this structure responds to cosmic expansion in a way that generates an effective dark energy contribution through its interaction with gravity.

In a recent development, “Our theoretical framework suggests no latest particles may be required at all,” states Professor Ariel Zhitnitsky of UBC’s Department of Physics and Astronomy, whose earlier theoretical work provided the foundation for the study. “The characteristic energy scale predicted from the QCD vacuum and gravity comes out close to the observed dark-energy scale today without having to introduce an ad-hoc new field nor new parameter.”.

Rather than introducing an adjustable parameter to reproduce the observed strength of dark energy, the framework derives its characteristic energy scale from established physical constants.

“The most striking result is that the observed dark-energy scale emerges naturally from known physical constants, without the need for any additional fitting parameters,” says UBC Professor Ludovic Van Waerbeke.

The researchers also investigated whether the framework could reproduce measurements of the Universe’s expansion history. Using astronomical observations, including light from distant exploding stars (supernovae) and radiation left over from the early Universe, they found that the model performed comparably to standard cosmological models in fitting the data.

“The idea that the quantum vacuum as described by QCD could have the right properties to account for the accelerated expansion of the universe is very intriguing,” says Dong Ha Lee, a PhD researcher at the University of Sheffield and lead author of the paper.

The analysis also indicates that the framework can reproduce the changing dark energy behavior suggested by current cosmological observations. Unlike a simple cosmological constant, which maintains a constant energy density over time, evolving dark energy models allow that density to change as the Universe expands.

“It raises the possibility that dark energy could be connected to the established theory of the strong nuclear force, without introducing latest fundamental fields. Testing models based on this idea against cosmological data is an essential step. Our analysis shows that such a model can reproduce the evolving dark energy behavior suggested by current observations. This motivates further theoretical work to better understand how the QCD vacuum responds to cosmic expansion and to develop predictions that can be tested with future observations.”.

Although the model agrees with existing astronomical measurements, that agreement does not establish that the QCD vacuum is responsible for dark energy. Further theoretical work is needed to clarify how its quantum structure interacts with cosmic expansion and whether the framework produces predictions that distinguish it from competing explanations.

The team plans to refine its calculations and compare the results with upcoming observations from next-generation space telescopes. More precise measurements of how the Universe has expanded over billions of years could help determine whether dark energy is connected to the same quantum physics that governs matter inside atomic nuclei.

Sources indicate that reference: “Evolving Dark Energy Is Vacuum Energy After All” by Dong Ha Lee, Carsten van de Bruck, Eleonora Di Valentino, Ludovic Van Waerbeke and Ariel Zhitnitsky, 20 November 2026, The Astrophysical Journal. DOI: 10.3847/1538-4357/aeb9cc.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that “The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” said Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., seen above. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday did little to quell bipartisan demands from Congress for an accounting of potential national security fallout from his affair with an alleged Chinese spy and talk of adding tougher chip export controls to the annual defense authorization bill.

Huang admitted on Sunday to having an affair, and reports say that it was with Alice Huang, an executive at Singaporean tech company and Nvidia customer Megaspeed, whom the U.S. government believes spied for China, according to recent reports. The New York Times and Reuters reported he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters Thursday that he supports the Senate investigating Huang’s potential influence on U.S. artificial intelligence and chip policy.

“I think that it would make sense because of the… nature of the association… and the governments and the national security interests we were talking about here,” Thune stated, though he said he thought it would be “wrong” to make assumptions about how close Huang’s relationship with President Donald Trump has been.

Sources indicate that senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., echoed the need for lawmakers to delve into the scandal, saying in a post on X that “Congress must demand answers.”.

Industry observers note that “The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Were government officials told not to investigate because of Trump’s relationship with Mr. Huang? What did Trump know when he personally invited Mr. Huang aboard Air Force One?” Schumer wrote, referring to the president having invited Huang to accompany him to China in May.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., remarked at a press conference that Reps. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., and Jim Himes, D-Conn., the ranking members of the Foreign Affairs and Intelligence committees, respectively, are leading Democrats’ efforts to “get to the bottom of what has happened.”.

“We need a classified briefing made available to members of Congress as it relates to the Nvidia situation,” Jeffries said. “And to the extent that our national security has been compromised, the American people deserve answers, and we're going to work to make sure that happens.”.

The investigations look likely to begin before control of Congress changes hands in January.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., who chairs the House select China committee, told reporters that his panel, along with House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence, are in negotiations with Huang to find a date for his testimony before Congress.

“The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” Moolenaar said. “What ways is Chinese intelligence influencing his perspective, his perspective influencing national security policy?”.

Industry observers note that last week, the chairs of the three committees sent a letter to Huang requesting that he appear at a joint closed-door briefing. Moolenaar stated that if Huang does not agree to a date, the committees will subpoena him.

It has been revealed that late Thursday, he joined with House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., and House Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark., in sending a fresh letter to Huang seeking a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 1. They also wrote to Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter seeking a similar interview on Dec. 2. Separately, Mast wrote to Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce Department undersecretary for industry and security, seeking his appearance at a committee hearing on Dec. 3.

Moolenaar also noted that Congress needs to understand what privileged information Chinese intelligence may have gained access to through Huang and how they may have tried to influence U.S. policy.

In a recent development, “We need to have strong safeguards when it comes to our technology and export controls,” Moolenaar said. “And [Huang has] been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls. This shines a whole newly introduced light on that discussion.”.

Recent findings suggest that also late Thursday, Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C.,  sent a letter to Huang calling on him to appear at a Dec. 3 committee hearing and another letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify at a Dec. 10 hearing "regarding recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns.".

A proposed manager’s amendment to the Senate's fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill (S 4784) contains several possibilities for those safeguards, including requirements for chip security mechanisms that would allow for verification if semiconductors are diverted to countries of concern and a ban on exporting certain very powerful chips to those countries. The House NDAA does not contain similar language.

Sources indicate that however, House Armed Services Chair Mike D. Rogers, D-Ala., is open to the restrictions. He told reporters Wednesday that he “would like to see” semiconductor export controls in the NDAA, but that the Huang scandal had not changed his position.

Democratic Caucus Vice Chair Ted Lieu, D-Calif., told reporters on Thursday that after reports that the federal government had been aware of Huang’s affair with the alleged spy, the administration should have shared the information with Congress.

“The administration needs to be investigated for hiding this information from Congress and the American people,” he said.

Lieu also suggested that Nvidia’s reported donation to the White House ballroom project influenced the Trump administration’s decision to allow the export of some powerful Nvidia chips to China.

It has been revealed that “There is no reason to do that. That hurts our national security, and we have an opportunity right now to fix that in the upcoming National Defense Authorization,” Lieu said.

Recent findings suggest that mast remarked the Huang revelations could give latest momentum to including chip export rules in the NDAA. He also said that his “directive” on the issue came “straight from the admin” and informed his objectives on the committee.

“Don't let chips be smuggled to China. Make sure that American companies get to buy them first,” Mast said. “Make sure that the machines that make them don't get sold to them, even though it's the Dutch that make the machines. Make sure that they can't access it remotely.”.

Mast’s committee has advanced many of those priorities, including some of the language included in the NDAA.

In March, the committee on a unanimous vote advanced legislation known as the Chip Security Act, which would require chip security mechanisms to verify that certain semiconductors subject to export controls aren’t diverted to countries of concern, including China and Iran.

The committee also advanced bills to require the Bureau of Industry and Security and the State Department to work with allied suppliers of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to implement export controls to prevent the equipment from going to countries of concern, and to require licenses for the export of certain powerful chips, including banning exporting certain chips to countries of concern.

Versions of all three bills are included in the Senate manager’s amendment to the NDAA.

The scandal has also led to calls for oversight of the Commerce Department, including Secretary Howard Lutnick, for its handling of export policy and actions around Huang.

Sources indicate that sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters Thursday that Lutnick and Nvidia should testify “before Democrats can set the narrative.”.

It has been revealed that “If there is some reasonable basis or some way to discount some of the reporting, the best way to do it is request a meeting with us and give us a briefing,” Tillis said. “Because otherwise, you're going to get what you get in an oversight hearing in about six weeks.”.

Asked about oversight of the Commerce Department’s role in the Huang scandal, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, who chairs the Commerce Committee, said his panel “has engaged in vigorous oversight under Republican presidents and Democrat presidents and will continue to be [engaged in it].”.

On Wednesday, prior to Huang’s resignation, Senate Banking ranking member Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller requesting that they “preserve all documents, communications, records, and other materials regarding the export of NVIDIA’s advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China.”.

“This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,” the senators wrote.

It has been revealed that in a statement Thursday, Warren stated that Huang’s resignation did not “absolve” him of the need to answer questions. She also called for the passage of stricter export controls, including the bill to ban the export of certain chips to China.

Industry observers note that sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., sent his own letter on Wednesday to Lutnick, Rubio, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, requesting an upgrade on the Justice Department’s investigation into Megaspeed for possibly diverting U.S. chips to China.

Scientists Successfully Grow Potatoes in Simulated Moon Soil

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (645 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Successful potato harvests in simulated lunar soil suggest that future astronauts could recycle their food scraps to help grow their next meal.
  • A future in which humans live on the Moon and grow their own food may be a little closer to reality thanks to one of Earth’s most familiar crops.
  • In a recent development, the findings support NASA’s Artemis program, which aims to establish a sustained human presence on the Moon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Successful potato harvests in simulated lunar soil suggest that future astronauts could recycle their food scraps to help grow their next meal.

A future in which humans live on the Moon and grow their own food may be a little closer to reality thanks to one of Earth’s most familiar crops. Researchers at Oregon State University have successfully grown edible potatoes in simulated lunar soil, achieving growth and yields comparable to those produced on Earth by adding compost made with the help of earthworms.

In a recent development, the findings support NASA’s Artemis program, which aims to establish a sustained human presence on the Moon. Producing food locally would reduce dependence on costly resupply missions from Earth and help make long-term lunar exploration more sustainable. Potatoes are particularly appealing because they provide substantial nutritional value and produce more calories per unit of land than many other crops.

“We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter,” mentioned Aymeric Goyer of Oregon State University’s Department of Botany and Plant Pathology. “That’s an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the Moon.”.

According to recent reports, one of the biggest agricultural challenges on the Moon lies directly beneath astronauts’ feet. Most of the lunar surface is covered in regolith, a layer of loose rock and dust containing very little organic matter.

In a study published in npj Microgravity, Goyer and his colleagues tested whether adding different amounts of vermicompost, a nutrient-rich material produced when earthworms break down organic matter, could make simulated lunar soil suitable for growing potatoes.

Because the composition of lunar regolith varies across the Moon, the team tested five simulants representing both the Moon’s darker plains, known as lunar maria, and its highland regions. For comparison, they included soil from Hermiston, Oregon, a region known for producing some of the highest potato yields in the world.

Potato plants grown in simulated lunar soil without compost were severely stunted and developed poorly formed roots. Adding between 5% and 15% vermicompost led to only partial recovery. However, plants grown with 30% vermicompost matched the growth and development of those cultivated in Earth soils.

Lunar regolith also contains elevated levels of heavy metals that can damage plant roots and interfere with growth.

“We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith by reducing plant exposure to harmful compounds,” said David Handy, a postdoctoral researcher in Goyer’s lab.

The researchers suspect that organic matter binds to heavy metals, making them less available to plants and limiting their harmful effects.

In a recent development, growing potatoes successfully would mean little if astronauts could not safely eat them. Encouragingly, potatoes produced in the lunar soil simulants maintained their nutritional quality and indicated no statistically significant increase in glycoalkaloids, naturally occurring potato toxins often associated with green discoloration beneath the skin. The findings indicate that the potatoes were safe to eat under the conditions tested.

Sources indicate that future lunar explorers could potentially bring a small supply of organic matter from Earth and gradually produce more by recycling food scraps and plant waste. Such a system could turn everyday waste into valuable growing material while reducing the supplies astronauts would need to transport from Earth.

Sources indicate that the research team is now investigating which potatoes might be best suited for lunar agriculture. A forthcoming paper will report results from experiments involving 10 potato varieties grown in simulated lunar soil.

In a recent development, reference: “Growth and molecular responses of potato to lunar regolith simulants” by David Handy, Anika Loeffler, Medora Knudson, Sydney Campbell, Pankaj Jaiswal, Jeffrey C. Anderson and Aymeric Goyer, 19 November 2026, npj Microgravity. DOI: 10.1038/s41526-026-00668-z.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Maya people had a toxic relationship with the color red—quite literally, according to fresh research. The upcoming analysis of the Yucatán Peninsula during the Maya era identified astronomically spiked levels of mercury, which might have contributed to the collapse of Maya culture.

“The mercury data was crazy,” Matt Waters, an environmental sciences professor and paleolimnologist at Auburn University, said in a university statement about the unexpected discovery on the peninsula. “Off the charts. These mercury levels aren’t normal.”.

Matt Waters led a study published in Science Advances that explored sediment samples collected at two lakes—Lago Coba and Cenote Xcach—showing the intense spike in mercury (Hg) levels ranging from around 40 C.E. to 800 C.E.

“We show that Classic Period Hg concentrations in sediment cores from two lakes on the Yucatán Peninsula exceeded modern sediment Hg toxicity thresholds by orders of magnitude for centuries during ancient Maya occupation,” the authors wrote, adding that the heightened pollution coincides with aquatic food collapse, “confirming that Hg toxicity was an additional environmental stressor for Classic Maya populations.”.

Sources indicate that while Waters isn’t saying mercury caused the collapse of the Maya civilization, he also doesn’t want to ignore its impact. “It’s been confirmed that drought was an concern, deforestation was an issue, erosion was an issue, overpopulation was an issue, and feeding the population was probably an issue,” he noted. “This study adds the impact of water quality. Let’s put that in the list. That’s what our study does. It establishes that list and moves it forward.”.

The study actually began as part of a National Science Foundation project focused on harmful algal blooms, but a then-graduate student and study co-author, Savanna Wooten, suggested also testing for heavy metals. Sediment coring from the lake bottoms pulled up mud from thousands of years ago that contained the intense mercury spikes during the Classic Maya Period, which were then followed by an abrupt decline.

The powerfully high mercury concentration lasted for hundreds of years, and Waters believes the sudden change at the base level likely moved up the food web, impacting fish and other larger creatures. Not only would eating fish or drinking water have exposed humans to the toxic levels, but there may have even been fewer fish to catch. “They would have seen a strange color change in the water,” Waters told Live Science, “and a drop in its productivity, such as fish for protein.”.

Waters linked to a study he’d worked on with a team from the University of Florida in the late 1990s that found a gap in ostracod shells during a specific period from Coba, correlating the missing shell timing to the rise in mercury. Further investigation into the cores found that declines in biological markers occurred throughout. “The algae was killed,” he said. “The cyanobacteria, they tanked. Purple sulfur bacteria, vanished. The biological community completely changed.”.

The people “experienced this for decades and, in one case, for centuries.”.

Sources indicate that the source of that mercury was cinnabar, they believe, a vibrant red mineral made up of 86 percent mercury that Maya culture viewed as a sacred pigment. “This was not like mercury raining down from the sky,” Waters mentioned. “This was not a regional thing. It was concentrated.”.

Maya loved cinnabar, using the bright red in pottery, murals, temple walls, and burials. To keep up with demand, they heavily imported it, especially around Coba and Xcach. “It’s common knowledge that there was trade in obsidian, in jade, and beautiful stones, and weaponry,” Waters stated. “I think this could start a conversation that cinnabar could have been a major trade commodity.”.

It may also show a highly toxic love affair that contributed to Maya struggles.

Three Ancient Cosmic Collisions May Explain Why the Moon Has Two Faces

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have narrowed down when three massive collisions reshaped the Moon, bringing them closer to understanding why its Earth-facing side looks so different from its far side.
  • Billions of years ago, a collision powerful enough to melt enormous quantities of lunar rock created the Moon’s largest impact basin.
  • It has been revealed that located on the Moon’s far side, the South Pole-Aitken (SPA) basin is one of the oldest and largest impact structures in the solar system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have narrowed down when three massive collisions reshaped the Moon, bringing them closer to understanding why its Earth-facing side looks so different from its far side.

Billions of years ago, a collision powerful enough to melt enormous quantities of lunar rock created the Moon’s largest impact basin. Subsequent collisions broke apart and scattered some of that ancient material across the surface, leaving behind a geological record that scientists are now piecing together.

It has been revealed that located on the Moon’s far side, the South Pole-Aitken (SPA) basin is one of the oldest and largest impact structures in the solar system. Understanding its history could help explain why the Moon’s near and far sides are so different, what lies beneath its surface, and when major collisions occurred during its early evolution.

It has been revealed that an international research team led by Professor Guochun Zhao, Mok Sau-King, a professor in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences (DEPS) at the University of Hong Kong (HKU), and Dr. Yuqi Qian, the study’s first author, has identified two types of magnesium-rich rocks with remarkably different origins. Published in Science Advances, the research also establishes a clearer timeline of the major impacts that shaped the region.

For decades, the basin remained largely unexplored. That changed in 2019, when Chang’e-4 completed the first successful landing on the Moon’s far side, followed in 2024 by Chang’e-6, which brought the first rock samples from this largely unexplored region back to Earth.

Using Chang’e-6 samples allocated to HKU DEPS and surface measurements from both missions, the researchers obtained the first direct geological evidence from the two landing sites for reconstructing the basin’s impact history. Satellite observations and numerical simulations helped them trace the origins of rocks across the wider basin.

One group of rocks, known as moderately magnesium-rich norites, formed in the aftermath of the original SPA collision. The impact generated a thick sheet of molten rock that gradually cooled, with different minerals crystallizing at different stages. Later collisions exposed these ancient rocks at the central peaks of large craters. Some were eventually blasted toward the Chang’e-4 landing site in Von Kármán crater by the impact that formed Finsen crater.

The second group contained considerably more magnesium and likely formed through a separate process called magnesium-suite magmatism, a type of magma activity associated with the original SPA impact. These rocks were exposed along the western ring of mountain peaks within the Apollo basin before the Chaffee S impact scattered some of them toward the Chang’e-6 landing site.

Recent findings suggest that earlier research by the HKU-led team had already uncovered evidence of prolonged volcanic activity and previously unrecognized magma activity in the region. Those studies also suggested that underground accumulations of titanium-rich minerals, known as ilmenite-bearing cumulates, helped account for the contrasting volcanic histories of the Moon’s two sides.

Sources indicate that the latest findings suggest that the South Pole-Aitken basin formed approximately 4.34 billion years ago. Another major collision created the Apollo basin around 4.2 billion years ago, followed by the formation of the Orientale basin approximately 3.87 billion years ago. Together, these three events reveal how successive collisions reshaped the Moon’s largest impact basin over hundreds of millions of years.

It has been revealed that reference: “Postimpact evolution of the South Pole–Aitken basin revealed by Chang’e-4 and Chang’e-6” by Yuqi Qian, Wenlei Song, James Head, Mingyu Tian, Zhuang Guo, Harald Hiesinger, Carolyn H. van der Bogert, Le Zhang, Jingyou Chen, Wanfeng Zhang, Ziqing Li, Lingzhi Sun, Xiangsong Wang, Wei-Ran Li, Jiacheng Liu, Nicolas Dauphas, Yi-Gang Xu and Guochun Zhao, 18 November 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeh9798.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Unfortunately, the risks of this technology are far from minuscule, including its impact on human education, the environment, and potentially the survival of the human race (an all-too-plausible scenario put forward by AI tech CEOs).
  • At least, that’s the latest conclusion by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), a nonpartisan watchdog housed in the legislative branch of the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the dawn of artificial intelligence brings with it both rewards and risks. With the ability to sift through unfathomably large data sets, AI could help detect cancers in their infancy, unlock some of the most enduring mysteries of mathematics, and even help contain the beating nuclear heart of future fusion reactors.

Unfortunately, the risks of this technology are far from minuscule, including its impact on human education, the environment, and potentially the survival of the human race (an all-too-plausible scenario put forward by AI tech CEOs). Even the everyday LLMs that now litter our digital lives—Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, and Grok—can aid and abet some of the most dangerous actors on the planet.

At least, that’s the latest conclusion by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), a nonpartisan watchdog housed in the legislative branch of the U.S. government. Typically, GAO turns its investigative gaze on efforts to limit fraud and wasteful spending in the government itself, but in a fresh tactic at the urging of U.S. Senator Maggie Hassan (D-NH), the office instead performed real-world tests on the platform to see if these four popular AI models would aid in planning a terrorist attack.

“A terrorist can log onto an AI platform and in less than 12 hours walk away with a concrete playbook for how to carry out a deadly attack,” Hassan, incoming Chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, stated in a press statement. “Today’s upcoming report makes it clear that the AI public safety threat is no longer theoretical.”.

Sources indicate that GAO conducted this test in the spring this year, and earlier this week reported some disturbing results. Two of the platforms, according to an official GAO release, provided guidance on building and detonating an improvised explosion device, or IED, and two other AI models showing differing methods for targeting the electrical grid. Within 12 hours, all four models also gamed through potential locations and methods for carrying out such an attack.

Industry observers note that although these violent lines of questioning triggered each platform’s safeguards, GAO got around them using common safeguard-bypassing techniques. Additionally, they confirmed the validity of the information provided with experts. The results of this investigation were published in a 61-page report that will be central to future senate hearings on AI safety.

“We set out to do two different types of evil,” GAO director Kevin Walsh noted in an interview posted on YouTube. “The first type is we wanted to create a bomb. And we didn’t just want to know how to create a bomb, we wanted it to help pick out a target, a location, and a time, and to give us instructions all the way…Evil scenario two, we wanted to do a bunch of economic damage, and in both cases that ended up being targeting the electrical grid.”.

In one case, Walsh reports that one AI model would refuse to answer questions or divert the user to more safe behaviors but said that “it wasn’t always successful.” Walsh notes that companies theoretically call law enforcement when suspicious activity is detected, but whether that occurs and at what frequency is uncertain.

Industry observers note that “As AI capabilities evolve, AI providers will continue to refine their safeguards,” the report concludes. “However, in its current state, this technology can potentially be dangerous and its misuse represents a growing risk to national and economic security.”.

The GAO officially released these terrorist-abetting findings on November 18, 2026, the same day Anthropic, creators of Claude, went public on the stock exchange. Despite the company’s own admission of AI being an existential threat to humanity, its IPO at one point reached a meteoric a $2 trillion valuation before dipping back down to a (measly) $1.6 trillion.

  • The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A group of visitors walks past the Capitol on Sept. 22. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo).

With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.

The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.

And it would bump funding for the Government Accountability Office up to $860 million, an increase of nearly 6 percent from fiscal 2026. That stands in contrast to the version of the bill advanced by the House Appropriations Committee in May, which floated slashing the GAO by 25 percent.

According to recent reports, it joins several other draft spending bills released this week by Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is trying to kickstart bicameral negotiations as lawmakers stare down a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government.

Her committee ran into a stalemate on topline numbers earlier this year that stopped it from marking up any of the 12 annual bills, but lawmakers nipped the threat of a government shutdown in the bud ahead of the midterm elections by pushing through a continuing resolution. With that funding now set to expire next month, appropriators are hoping they can wrap up at least some of the bills while punting the rest into the next Congress with another stopgap.

In a recent development, the Legislative Branch bill is the smallest of the 12 appropriations bills and typically among the least controversial. But debates over the GAO have become a sticking point during the Trump administration as the agency accuses the White House of violating budget laws — a move the Office of Management and Budget has pushed back on, arguing the GAO has no authority over the administration since it is part of the legislative branch.

In a recent development, the GAO has been without a permanent head after its longtime leader Gene L. Dodaro retired last year, although Republicans are now making a last-ditch effort to get one confirmed during the lame-duck session before Democrats take power.

The House version of the spending bill sought to bar the comptroller general from suing under the 1974 budget law restricting presidential impoundments, unless specifically authorized by Congress. But the Senate proposal includes no such language, and overall, it appears designed to avoid drastic or contentious moves.

It would also leave in place a provision that would block cost-of-living adjustments for members of Congress, whose pay has been frozen since 2009.

Senate Democrats, however, criticized the bill text after its release, saying it wouldn’t invest enough in the legislative branch.

“The Legislative Branch bill underfunds key work to support oversight of the Executive Branch, and it underfunds notable efforts to keep the Capitol complex safe,” Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., said in a statement.

The Architect of the Capitol would get $762.5 million, though funding for House office buildings is not included in that total. The agency is requesting $1.6 billion as it seeks to begin large-scale renovations of the Rayburn House Office Building. The architect has repeatedly warned lawmakers that parts of the Capitol complex are in need of critical infrastructure upgrades, arguing that delaying renovations will only make them more expensive as things continue to deteriorate.

The bill’s $5.3 billion proposal represents funding for the Senate and legislative branch agencies, while excluding House-only funds, which are typically added later.

Experimental Drug Shrinks Tumors in Two of the Hardest-To-Treat Cancers

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A single experimental drug designed to block signals from several cancer-driving mutations has shown encouraging early results, raising the possibility of treating multiple hard-to-treat cancers.
  • When pancreatic or lung cancer continues to grow despite several treatments, doctors can find themselves with few remaining options.
  • Sources indicate that the drug targets RAS, a family of genes that provide instructions for making proteins involved in controlling cell growth and division.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A single experimental drug designed to block signals from several cancer-driving mutations has shown encouraging early results, raising the possibility of treating multiple hard-to-treat cancers.

When pancreatic or lung cancer continues to grow despite several treatments, doctors can find themselves with few remaining options. In some patients, the difficulty lies in genetic mutations that keep cancer cells growing and have historically been difficult to target with drugs. An experimental cancer drug called ERAS-0015 has shown promising results in an early clinical trial, shrinking tumors in patients who had already undergone other forms of treatment.

Sources indicate that the drug targets RAS, a family of genes that provide instructions for making proteins involved in controlling cell growth and division. In healthy cells, RAS proteins act like molecular switches, turning on when cells receive signals to grow and turning off when those signals are no longer needed. Certain genetic mutations can leave these switches stuck in the “on” position, continuously instructing cells to grow and helping sustain cancer.

For years, scientists struggled to develop drugs capable of interfering with these faulty proteins. ERAS-0015 takes an approach known as a pan-RAS molecular glue. It works by bringing proteins together at the molecular level and is designed to bind to RAS while the switch is active, blocking growth signals associated with several different cancer-driving RAS mutations.

It has been revealed that “The overall goal of precision oncology is to match a patient’s mutation, or the ‘Achilles Heel’ of a specific individual’s cancer, to a drug that directly targets that mutation. This is what we are attempting to do by studying the effectiveness of ERAS-0015 in patients with RAS alterations,” stated Dr. Judy Wang, a medical oncologist at Florida Cancer Specialists and Research Institute in Sarasota, Florida.

Wang presented findings from 148 patients participating in the phase I AURORAS-1 clinical trial on November 19, 2026, at the 38th EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona, Spain.

Recent findings suggest that the trial began in June 2025 and is evaluating ERAS-0015 both alone and in combination with other anticancer therapies. Participants include people with pancreatic cancer, colorectal (bowel) cancer, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that has spread beyond the original tumor site, and other solid tumors driven by RAS mutations. The results presented at the symposium included 83 patients with pancreatic cancer and 37 with NSCLC. The trial is continuing to enroll patients.

Recent findings suggest that “AURORAS-1 has enrolled patients that have tried a number of other treatments for their cancer. In this context, ERAS-0015 treatment caused a 44% response rate in patients with RAS-mutant pancreatic cancer and a 60% response rate in patients with RAS-mutant lung cancer. A ‘response’ means the patients experienced considerable tumor shrinkage, and these response rates are key as they show clinically meaningful activity from ERAS-0015 treatment in patient groups that have few if any therapeutic options to address their cancer. In addition to this, ERAS-0015 was well tolerated with few severe side effects,” Wang told the symposium.

These response rates came from relatively small groups of patients receiving a 32 mg dose of the drug. Tumors shrank in 11 of 25 patients with pancreatic cancer who had previously received chemotherapy and in three of five patients with lung cancer who had previously been treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors, drugs that help the immune system recognize and attack cancer, or platinum-based chemotherapy.

Sources indicate that researchers gradually increased doses of ERAS-0015 from 2 mg to 40 mg to evaluate how well patients tolerated the drug. After a median follow-up of just over four months, there was no indication that the maximum tolerated dose had been reached.

At doses of 16 to 32 mg, the most common side effects, affecting at least 10% of patients, were rash, diarrhea, nausea, and inflammation of the lining of the mouth. Twelve patients (9.8%) experienced severe treatment-related side effects, classified as grade 3 or higher. No dose-limiting side effects were reported.

“We are encouraged by the preliminary clinical activity and tolerability of ERAS-0015 in patients that have tried a number of other treatments for RAS-driven lung and pancreatic cancer,” said Wang.

“Our goal is to give clinicians upcoming, better options for treating their patients with RAS-driven cancers. Early results suggest ERAS-0015 has the potential to be one of these options.”.

Phase I clinical trials involve relatively small numbers of patients and are primarily designed to evaluate safety and determine appropriate doses. Although the tumor shrinkage observed in this trial provides an early indication of the drug’s potential, larger phase II and phase III clinical trials will be necessary to confirm its safety and effectiveness.

“If these early results are confirmed, ERAS-0015 could offer patients with RAS-driven cancers a upcoming option. Clinical development of ERAS-0015 would be impossible without the patients, caregivers, investigators and participating trial centers that put their trust in us to take part in our study. We are deeply grateful for their contribution to AURORAS-1,” Wang concluded.

Sources indicate that professor Elena Garralda, chair of the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium and co-director of the Vall d’Hebron Institute of Oncology’s clinical research program, was not involved in the study. She commented: “This is the first presentation of these preliminary results from the AURORAS-1 clinical trial and they have been eagerly awaited. They show that the RAS inhibitor, ERAS-0015, has encouraging anti-tumor activity in cancers that are hard to treat successfully and for which there are few treatment options available. We look forward to further results from larger clinical trials, which are investigating whether ERAS-0015 can help a broader group of patients.

“This is one of several studies being presented at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium that are beginning to show it is possible to design drugs that target cancers driven by RAS mutations, which was not thought possible until recently.”.

Meeting: 38th EORTC-NCI-AACR SYMPOSIUM.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The fossil fuel industry is the largest contributor to climate change, and it’s not even close.
  • Despite this unwillingness to change, some companies are trying to find ways to make some good out of a bad situation.
  • In a recent development, instead of making fuel at a massive refinery and transporting it long distances, the system is designed to produce fully formulated synthetic jet or diesel fuel closer to where it will be used,” Nick Steinke, the tech giant’s director of programs, government and defense, remarked in a recent interview with Waste360.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The fossil fuel industry is the largest contributor to climate change, and it’s not even close. According to the United Nations, the industry is responsible for 68 percent of all greenhouse gas emissions and an incredible 90 percent of all carbon dioxide emissions. Stick a stake in the vampiric heart of fossil fuels, and beating back the worst effects of global warming becomes suddenly much more possible. But as the recent climate summit at Antalya, Türkiye, this month displayed, the industry highlights no interest in giving up its polluting ways, leading some countries to say the world is now “held hostage by the oil mafia.”.

Despite this unwillingness to change, some companies are trying to find ways to make some good out of a bad situation. One of those companies AIRCO (originally named Air Company), based out of Fresh Britain, Pennsylvania, did just that by developing a technology that creates jet fuel of a thin “air”—well, kind of.

In a recent development, instead of making fuel at a massive refinery and transporting it long distances, the system is designed to produce fully formulated synthetic jet or diesel fuel closer to where it will be used,” Nick Steinke, the tech giant’s director of programs, government and defense, remarked in a recent interview with Waste360. “It takes captured CO₂ and hydrogen and integrates the conversion process into a modular, containerized system.”.

Instead of relying on centralized fuel producers, the idea is that synthetic fuels could be created on-site where they’ll be used directly, circumventing the climate impacts of transporting the fuel entirely. Also the ingredients AIRCO uses also aims to come from green sources by leveraging carbon capture technologies for the required CO2 and using electrolysis to supply hydrogen from water.

Chemical & Engineering News reported earlier this year the company hopes to supply the U.S. military with a complete reactor system by 2027 that will be powered on a government site using a small nuclear reactor (SMR), and supply a sufficient flow of energy required for both carbon capture and electrolysis to provide the volumes of ingredients needed to make these mobile, fuel-creating systems viable. It’s a task that at least one expert notes sounds easier noted than done.

“The technology seems like it holds a lot of promise, especially on the fuel-conversion side, but the part that I have a lot of questions about is, where are you getting the carbon from?” Sarah Gleeson, a materials scientist at Project Drawdown, told WHYY, a local radio station. “Because if they’re saying that there’s some kind of direct air capture functionality in this really mobile device, I would be skeptical at the capacity and efficiency of it.”.

Carbon capture is central to the company’s promise of its technology’s carbon-neutral nature with the company’s CEO telling WHYY that “using more CO2 in our production process to make the fuel than we are putting out in the entire process.” Carbon capture, as a broad technology category, still remains unproved even as some climate models rely on its implementation (and the fact that the oil industry likes the technology is concerning to say the least).

If humanity hopes to secure a healthy planet for future generations, ending its reliance on fossil fuels is priority number one. But step one in the process is first limiting—and eventually eliminating— latest fuel from being extracted from the ground in the first place while the advancements in green chemistry try to put to work the carbon dioxide that’s already here.
