The prickly pear cactus has a surprising trick for surviving in the desert

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1319 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have discovered that tiny, short-lived leaves help prickly pear cacti capture carbon during the day and accelerate growth.
  • Cacti are usually described as plants that replaced their leaves with spines and thick green stems.
  • When rain finally reaches the desert, though, the prickly pear sprouts small green leaves on each newly introduced pad.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have discovered that tiny, short-lived leaves help prickly pear cacti capture carbon during the day and accelerate growth.

Cacti are usually described as plants that replaced their leaves with spines and thick green stems.

When rain finally reaches the desert, though, the prickly pear sprouts small green leaves on each newly introduced pad. Within a few weeks, these are shed again.

A team in Israel found that these leaflets behave like the leaves of a common garden plant. Carbon dioxide is taken in by them during the day.

The researchers estimate that they supply about a fifth of the carbon a young pad needs for growth.

So the cactus has two ways of gathering carbon rather than one. Older pads collect it after sunset, and the leaflets add to the supply once the sun is up.

The research was conducted by scientists at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev (BGU) in Israel. They worked with researchers from the Gilat Research Center of the Volcani Institute.

It has been revealed that potted plants of Opuntia ficus-indica were grown for the experiments. This is the prickly pear species that is cultivated on farms.

Sources indicate that the plants were kept in a net house on BGU’s desert campus at Sde Boker. They were watered every day for a year.

Ilya Gelfand is a professor at BGU’s Jacob Blaustein Institutes for Desert Research and a co-author of the study.

“The cactus effectively has two gears,” said Gelfand. “Most of the year it runs in saving mode and breathes at night to hold on to every drop.”.

“When water arrives, it switches on a second, faster gear: temporary leaves that work by day like a regular plant. When the good times end, it simply drops them.”.

In most plants the tiny pores on the leaves are opened during the day.

According to recent reports, carbon dioxide enters through them and is used by the plant to build sugars. Water is lost through the same openings, and that loss becomes costly in hot desert conditions.

Cacti, agave and many other succulents get by on less water because their pores open at night instead. The carbon dioxide is stored as an acid until the following morning.

The pores then close, and carbon dioxide released from the stored acid is used to make sugars with the help of sunlight.

According to recent reports, this strategy is known as crassulacean acid metabolism or CAM. Mature prickly pear pads rely on it so heavily that scientists classify the species as a full-time CAM plant.

The prickly pear is also an important crop that is grown on about 6.4 million acres (2.6 million hectares) worldwide.

Recent findings suggest that much of this area lies in drought-prone parts of Africa and South America. In these regions the plant is used for food and livestock feed and for slowing desertification.

Recent findings suggest that until this project, nobody had examined the leaflets as working organs. Each one measures only about 0.4 inch (10 millimeters) in length.

Around 150 of them can be carried by a single latest pad, and they fall off after about six weeks.

Industry observers note that the study was led by Patrick Mdemba, who is a doctoral student at BGU. Pores were the first thing he and his colleagues examined.

Recent findings suggest that clear nail polish was brushed onto pads and leaflets at five different times of the day. After the polish had dried it was peeled away and examined under a microscope. Each thin film preserved an impression of the pore openings.

The older pads opened their pores at night, which was the expected result for a CAM plant. The leaflets revealed the opposite pattern. Their pores were opened in the morning and closed after dark, as in a typical leafy plant.

Sources indicate that young pads that were two weeks old did not follow either pattern. Their pores were found to be open at every time the team checked.

Acid build-up between dusk and dawn was then measured in each tissue. A large amount was stored overnight in the older pads.

The young pads stored more acid as they grew older. In the leaflets no significant difference was seen between the dawn and dusk readings.

Recent findings suggest that mdemba’s team also looked at the carbon inside the leaflets. Carbon in nature comes in a lighter form and a heavier form. Cactus pads that feed at night build up more of the heavier one.

In week-old leaflets the carbon looked much like the carbon in the pads. The mother pad had probably supplied it. Five weeks later the leaflets held noticeably more of the lighter form that daytime leaves collect.

For a second test the researchers sealed whole plants in a clear box almost 4 feet wide. They filled it with carbon dioxide made from the heavier form. One run lasted from 10 a.m. until noon, after the pads had closed their pores.

Industry observers note that the marked carbon was found in the leaflets. The pads on those same plants gained no significant amount.

Next came leaflets with no pad at all. Mdemba cut them from pads less than a week old and kept them in sealed jars on a sugar-free gel.

In sunlight the carbon dioxide in each jar went down. Under aluminum foil it went back up. The cut leaflets also grew heavier until about day 15.

Mature pads in an earlier study took in carbon dioxide about twice as fast per square inch as the leaflets.

Mature pads in an earlier study took in carbon dioxide about twice as fast per square inch.

The team then worked out a carbon budget. A pad with about 150 leaflets gets roughly 0.12 grams of carbon a day from them. A 1998 study put a growing pad’s daily need near 0.6 grams. So the leaflets supply about 20% of it.

The leaflets covered their own growth first. What was left over went to the young pad.

It has been revealed that mdemba then took the leaflets away. All of them were cut off some young pads. On other pads they were left on but painted with clear nail polish, which sealed their pores.

Industry observers note that pad size was checked every five days. By day 25 both groups were about a third smaller in area than normal pads. Pads with no leaflets also weighed about 38% less at three weeks.

Without working leaflets, then, a newly introduced pad grew more slowly.

“That lets the cactus grow quickly whenever the desert briefly allows it, without giving up its ability to survive drought,” noted Gelfand.

Desert rain tends to arrive in short bursts. For desert plants the timing of that water can matter a great deal.

According to recent reports, some desert shrubs drop their leaves when life gets hard. The prickly pear makes its leaflets in the wet weeks and drops them within about two months.

It has been revealed that every plant in the study got water daily. That may have made the leaflets look more notable than they would be in a dry field. Well-watered pads may rely less on their night feeding.

Sources indicate that the authors listed other limits too. They did not measure the two enzymes that capture carbon in each system. Gas exchange was not followed over a full 24 hours. Their conclusions come from pores, acid and carbon tracers instead.

They recommend measuring those enzymes in leaflets and young pads, along with gas readings around the clock.

Recent findings suggest that plants under drought stress should be tested as well. That work could show how much the leaflets matter when a wet spell is short.

The full study was published in the Journal of Experimental Botany.

Industry News: Older adults don’t need to lift heavy weights to build strength

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1185 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Strength training with lighter weights may help older adults build strength and maintain muscle mass without heavy lifting.
  • Recent findings suggest that strength training is recommended for older adults to help maintain muscle, balance and independence.
  • Earlier research has reported that pain and high physical demands can lead older adults to drop out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Strength training with lighter weights may help older adults build strength and maintain muscle mass without heavy lifting.

Recent findings suggest that strength training is recommended for older adults to help maintain muscle, balance and independence. Heavy loads are commonly used in these programs.

Earlier research has reported that pain and high physical demands can lead older adults to drop out. The authors note that those who drop out often have traits associated with frailty.

A pilot trial in Perth, Western Australia, compared heavy training with lighter training in 40 adults over 55. Strength increased in both groups over 12 weeks.

Neither group showed a measurable change in muscle mass.

Industry observers note that the study was led by Brett Buist of the School of Human Sciences at the University of Western Australia. Training intensity was chosen by the participants rather than assigned at random.

“Both high- and lower-intensity resistance exercise appears equally effective at improving muscle strength while maintaining muscle mass and quality of life in older adults,” Buist noted.

Frailty has been linked to falls, hospital admissions, disability and death. Low physical activity and the loss of muscle mass and strength are listed among its common contributors.

The condition is not always permanent. Ohio State University’s guide to frailty states that it can often be slowed or improved with support.

Low strength is reflected in poorer walking and balance. These changes are known to raise the risk of a fall in older adults.

World Health Organization figures cited in the paper put the share of people over 60 at 12% in 2015. That share is projected to reach 22% by 2050.

Lifting weights appears on the National Institute on Aging’s list of strength exercises. The Perth study examined how heavy those weights need to be.

Sources indicate that of the 40 recruits, 33 were women. All participants were living independently in the community.

Industry observers note that sessions were held twice a week at the university under the supervision of exercise physiologists or physiotherapists. Every session included a leg press, a deadlift and a bench press.

Drop jumps from a low box were also performed in each session. The box was about 4 inches (10 centimeters) high, and each landing delivered a firm impact through both feet.

Sources indicate that A four-week introductory phase at low-to-moderate intensity was completed by all participants. From week five each person could either move to the heavy program or continue at the lighter level.

In both groups the sets were ended while two to five more repetitions could still have been completed.

The number of sets multiplied by repetitions was matched closely between the two programs. In this way the load on the bar remained the main difference.

To be classified as a heavy lifter, a participant had to leg press more than 80% of their estimated maximum. That level had to be reached in at least three out of every four sessions.

Twelve participants met this standard and 14 trained at the lighter level.

By the end of the trial both groups were able to press more weight with their chests and legs. Strength was assessed using the one-repetition maximum, which is the heaviest weight a person can lift once.

According to recent reports, increases in chest press, leg press and leg press relative to body weight were found in each group. Substantial loads were still handled by the lighter group.

It has been revealed that leg press loads in that group averaged about 71% of maximum. Deadlift effort was rated at a median of 5 on a 10-point scale.

According to recent reports, earlier reviews of research in older adults have generally favored heavy lifting for building strength. In some of the studies behind them, heavy training was compared with loads as low as 20% of maximum.

According to Buist’s team, loads that low were probably insufficient to increase strength. Unequal amounts of total work have also complicated earlier comparisons.

Leg press strength relative to body weight was the only outcome that differed significantly between the groups. However, the authors advised caution when interpreting this result.

“Clinicians can target factors that contribute to frailty using resistance exercise with intensity tailored to individual preferences without compromising outcomes,” said Buist.

Recent findings suggest that neither group indicated a measurable gain in muscle. Lean mass measured by whole-body X-ray scans stayed close to baseline in both programs.

This stability was viewed by the researchers as a useful result because lean mass usually declines with age.

Sources indicate that lean tissue already accounted for about 64% of the volunteers’ body weight at the start. This proportion was higher than in a comparison study cited by the authors.

No protein supplements were provided during the trial. The training volume was modest as well, with 12 working sets in each session. Some studies that did produce muscle growth used as many as 39 sets.

A small reduction in body fat as a share of total weight was observed in the lighter group. Higher general health scores on the SF-36 survey were reported by the heavy group.

Recent findings suggest that other scores on the questionnaire changed very little in either group. Most volunteers began between the 50th and 75th percentiles for Australians of their age and sex.

Postural sway was measured on a force plate during standing trials of 30 seconds each. After training the recorded sway path was longer under some of the test conditions.

It has been revealed that A longer sway path is normally taken as a sign of poorer balance. However, scores on the 14-item Berg Balance Scale did not decline and balance confidence was maintained.

The authors suggest that participants may have been exploring their limits of stability. Resistance training is known to extend those limits.

According to recent reports, the participants who completed the trial were not the group of greatest concern. Of the 39 people tested at baseline, 12 withdrew for reasons including joint pain and holidays.

An average baseline weight of about 162 pounds (73.7 kilograms) was recorded for those who withdrew. Participants who stayed averaged 133 pounds (60.4 kilograms) and had greater leg strength relative to body weight.

Heavier and weaker adults are of particular concern in frailty research, and they were overrepresented among the dropouts.

The final analysis included only 26 people, so small differences between the groups may have been missed. Physical activity outside the supervised sessions was not recorded.

Bonnie Furzer, a co-author from the University of Western Australia, presented the findings as guidance for those who prescribe exercise.

“For older adults who are not tolerating high-intensity resistance and impact training, lowering exercise intensity should be considered to assist adherence whilst maintaining benefits,” said Furzer.

Longer trials and studies in frail adults have been recommended by the authors.

Until that evidence is available, a weight that people continue to lift may matter more than the heaviest one possible.

The full study was published in the journal Translational Exercise Biomedicine.

Birdsong has more in common with human speech than scientists expected

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1047 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A comparison of 367 bird species and 52 human languages reveals unexpected similarities in the rhythms and patterns of vocal communication.
  • Recent findings suggest that birds and humans share some surprisingly similar patterns when they make sounds.
  • The finding comes from a comparison of the songs of 367 bird species with people speaking and singing in 52 languages.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A comparison of 367 bird species and 52 human languages reveals unexpected similarities in the rhythms and patterns of vocal communication.

Recent findings suggest that birds and humans share some surprisingly similar patterns when they make sounds. Even birds that never learn their songs naturally produce rhythms much like those found in human speech and music.

The finding comes from a comparison of the songs of 367 bird species with people speaking and singing in 52 languages.

Three patterns of human speech and music appeared across the birds, in those that learn their songs and in those that don’t.

The authors interpret that as a sign that the patterns come from the shared mechanics of making sound rather than from learning alone.

Logan James of McGill University and the University of Texas at Austin led the work with Jon Sakata of McGill. Several co-authors work at McGill’s Centre for Research on Brain, Language and Music.

In an interview with Earth.com, James noted that the shared patterns were what excited the team most.

“These results highlight that, despite the tremendous diversity across human languages and hundreds of species of birds, there are still fundamental shared sequencing patterns,” he stated.

In a recent development, the recordings came from xeno-canto, where birders around the world upload recordings. The team kept only recordings the recordist had rated top quality and labeled as song rather than calls.

No second species could be in the background, no playback could have been used to provoke the bird, and the singer had to have been seen.

Industry observers note that software then split each song into its separate sounds, and experienced annotators checked every sound. That work produced more than 74,500 individual sounds from about 5,900 songs.

The researchers paired each group of vocal learners with closely related birds that do not learn their songs: songbirds with suboscines, and hummingbirds with nightjars.

On the human side, the team used recordings of people speaking and singing in 52 languages, made for an earlier project.

In human speech and song, the pitch rarely leaps far from one syllable to the next. The team measured the pitch at the end of each bird sound and the start of the next.

Across the birds, the jumps were smaller than chance would produce.

Human voices also keep a beat, with sounds spaced evenly in time.

Birdsong showed the same pattern more often than would be expected by chance.

And people generally stretch the last sound of a phrase, the way a singer holds a final note.

Recent findings suggest that birds did that too. Their songs also tended to grow louder through the middle of a phrase and fade at the end, as human music does.

In a recent development, songbirds have been the usual comparison for human speech because they, like us, learn their songs by listening. This study could set them against close relatives that don’t.

Sakata told Earth.com that the team expected birds that learn their songs to show greater similarities to human speech, since people also learn to speak.

“What surprised us was that the songs of birds that do not learn their songs (e.g., suboscines, nightjars) actually had comparable patterns to us relative to the vocal-learning birds,” he stated.

It has been revealed that where vocal learning did make a difference, it did not act the same way in songbirds as in hummingbirds. The authors counted that as no consistent effect.

According to recent reports, the matches were not perfect. Unlike human voices, which tended to become quieter throughout a phrase, birdsong tended to grow louder in the middle before fading at the end.

The authors suspect breathing explains part of it.

A person usually speaks or sings a whole phrase on one breath, and they suggest that is why the volume drops toward the end. Birds take tiny breaths between the sounds in a song.

Sources indicate that lung size may matter too. Across the birds, bigger species stretched their final sounds more, and a human has much bigger lungs than any of them.

But nightjars, among the largest birds in the study, stretched their final sounds even more than people do, so size can’t explain all of it.

The team also ran a broader measurement of how pitch and rhythm change together across a whole phrase, the same one that separates speech from song in human recordings.

Industry observers note that by that measure, bird songs as a group were closer to human speech than to human singing. Hummingbirds and suboscines came out nearest to both, closer than the songbirds.

James noted no large group of birds was closest to human patterns overall.

A few species were, on that combined measure, among them the scaled antbird, the blackhead antbird and the rufous-tailed hummingbird.

Songbirds and suboscines did keep a steadier beat than hummingbirds and nightjars, so they are the better birds to study for the roots of human rhythm.

In a commentary published alongside the study, Kazuo Okanoya of Teikyo University wrote that the work gives researchers a basis for testing the mechanisms behind the shared patterns.

“Linguistic concepts can guide such tests but should not be used in place of experimental data,” he added.

The study was based entirely on recordings, so the researchers could not confirm whether similarities in how birds and humans produce sound explain the shared patterns.

It also remains unclear whether listeners’ preferences help shape these patterns.

Sakata said very little is known about the shape of the voice box in many of these species, and that mapping that variety is a next step.

James said earlier work by the group found that people tend to like the same male courtship sounds that females of that species like.

“So we are also curious to examine how much birds (and humans) like the sound of patterns that conform to these universal patterns,” James said.

Recent findings suggest that other features of human music, such as distinct notes and nested layers of structure, have not been checked in birds yet. The authors wrote that those are the next measurements to take.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

Latest Update: Gabe Evans reveals 2028 comeback bid from Boebert’s district

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Gabe Evans, who lost reelection earlier this month, announced Monday a 2028 run from the neighboring district of fellow defeated Republican Rep.
  • “Now more than ever, Colorado needs conservatives in Congress who will fight to keep our border secure, cut taxes for working families, keep boys from dominating girls' sports and locker rooms, protect our water, and make energy affordable,” Evans said in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rep. Gabe Evans, here arriving at the Capitol in July for a House Republican Conference meeting, lost his bid for a second term representing Colorado's 8th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

Colorado Rep. Gabe Evans, who lost reelection earlier this month, announced Monday a 2028 run from the neighboring district of fellow defeated Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert.

“Now more than ever, Colorado needs conservatives in Congress who will fight to keep our border secure, cut taxes for working families, keep boys from dominating girls' sports and locker rooms, protect our water, and make energy affordable,” Evans said in a statement.

His announcement comes less than two weeks after he lost his bid for a second term representing the battleground 8th District in the Denver area. While the race had been considered one of the most competitive in the country, Democratic former state Rep. Manny Rutinel secured victory by 15 points.

Sources indicate that as part of House Democrats’ massive midterm gains, they flipped three seats in Colorado. Boebert narrowly lost her reelection bid in the 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, while Republican Rep. Jeff Crank lost in the 5th District.

Evans’ statement cited his ties to the 4th District, which encompasses the eastern part of the state and extends into the Denver metro area.

“From Loveland to Lamar, I’m ready to keep fighting in the 4th District, where I grew up, and where my family has lived since 1976,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that the district has a deep history of voting Republican. Boebert won by 11 points in 2024 while Donald Trump carried the district by 18 points.

Evans is far from the first member of Congress to switch to a district seen as more favorable to his party. Boebert herself shifted from Colorado's more competitive 3rd District to run for the heavily conservative 4th in 2024.

The 4th District will likely be a top target for Republicans in 2028, and Evans’ campaign sought to portray him as a clear front-runner in what could become a crowded GOP primary.

Industry observers note that laubacher, a Navy veteran who will take office on Jan. 3, is the first Democrat elected to represent the 4th District since Betsy Markey won her lone term in 2008. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

As if leopards and saber-toothed cats weren’t enough, some ancient human relatives probably also had to contend with predators that swooped down from the skies.Adult male baboon remains found in Africa carry telltale signs of raptor predation. The specimens probably weighed about 22 to 26 kilograms in life. That’s twice the size of the largest primates previously known to be preyed upon by a raptor species and on par with some early human ancestors, researchers report November 18 in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology. Guarding against aerial predators may have pressured humans’ ancient cousins to form tighter social groups and develop vocal strategies that preceded language, the researchers say.

Industry observers note that biologists discovered the baboon bones among the high sandstone cliffs of Ennedi Plateau in northeastern Chad. These baboons (Papio anubis) have developed unique survival strategies, such as scaling 50-meter cliffs and digging for water and food. They share the plateau with multiple birds of prey, and the researchers have identified one as the most likely baboon hunter: the Verreaux’s eagle (Aquila verreauxii).

Sources indicate that researchers have long studied predation from land carnivores such as significant cats and crocodiles as a primary driver of behavioral changes in primates, including human ancestors. While a five-kilogram bird like a Verreaux’s eagle taking down a 22-kilogram monkey may seem unlikely, the raptors appear to have developed specialized hunting techniques.

“It’s pretty brutal, but it’s pretty quick,” says Cat Hobaiter, a primatologist at the University of St Andrews in Scotland. The eagles stab their talons “straight through the eye, straight through the brain, and that’s a very effective control and kill.” The birds may also drag the baboons off the cliffs, a strategy that golden eagles use to hunt large mountain goats and sheep in the Alps. The birds then dismember the prey and carry off pieces to their nests.

Industry observers note that three adult male baboon skulls that Hobaiter and her colleagues studied had clearly visible punctures through the eye sockets. And two specimens also had gashes across the shoulder bones, which appear to have been made by grasping talons. The researchers estimated the weight of the animals based on the size of the head of their femurs, where these upper leg bones attach to the hip.

While the punctures could come from something other than an eagle’s talon, such as a bite or a bullet, the clean circular holes in the skulls match similar damage to smaller monkeys hunted by eagles, Hobaiter states.

Sources indicate that “I found the evidence pretty compelling,” indicates Scott McGraw, an evolutionary biologist at Ohio State University in Columbus who was not involved with the work. The punctures look “remarkably similar” to injuries in monkeys hunted by the African crowned eagle in the Taï Forest of Côte d’Ivoire, McGraw says.

Sources indicate that the eagles also use the landscape to their advantage, hugging cliffs to stay hidden and possibly hunting in pairs, Hobaiter says. It’s possible that one eagle could distract the baboons from above while another swoops up from below a cliff to attack, as has been observed against other prey, she says.

While the research team did not witness an eagle attack a baboon, they did observe the monkeys responding to the Verreaux’s eagles’ presence, though not to other raptors in the area.

When the eagles flew down over a ridge, the baboons immediately barked out an alarm call and climbed over the edge of a cliff to safety, Hobaiter says.

The eagles’ ability to hunt large primates suggests that raptors may have also hunted ancient human ancestors, Hobaiter claims. In particular, the genus Australopithecus, which lived about 4 million to 2 million years ago and included the famous fossil named Lucy, had similar body sizes to the baboons. A 2.8-million-year-old skull called the Taung child from the species A. africanus even has puncture and scratch marks that McGraw and other researchers argue probably came from a raptor.

The threat from birds of prey paints a more complete picture of how and why our ancestors developed certain behaviors, such as social grouping to protect younger animals. Primates also use a range of vocal alerts to warn the group of danger. They use different sounds or combinations of sounds for different threats, such as a predator on the ground or in the sky.

“Those first steps towards combining information in different ways to be more specific … would have been a really important precursor [of language],” Hobaiter says.

  • It has been revealed that the nomination fills in the blanks after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., had scheduled a Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eric Ueland, No. 2 official at the White House Office of Management and Budget, arrives for his confirmation hearing in the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on April 3, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

President Donald Trump on Monday nominated Eric Ueland, deputy director for management in the White House budget office, to be the next comptroller general to lead the Government Accountability Office.

It has been revealed that the nomination fills in the blanks after Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., had scheduled a Nov. 19 hearing to examine more than a dozen of Trump’s nominees for executive and judicial positions but without identifying who the comptroller general candidate would be. Ueland's name has since been added to the hearing agenda.

The move sets up an unprecedented scenario where a top official of the Office of Management and Budget, a White House office that has tangled with the Government Accountability Office since Trump’s first term, is put forward as the next head of the legislative agency.

The GAO, a congressional watchdog with some 3,000 employees, has repeatedly accused the administration of violating the 1974 budget law by withholding or "impounding" enacted, appropriated funds. In September, for example, the GAO stated Trump’s cancellation of $810 million in spending without the approval of Congress through a so-called pocket rescission was illegal.

Industry observers note that white House Budget Director Russ Vought was quick to respond on X, writing that GAO “has become hyper partisan and ... they make their legal assessments based on whether Democrats are in the White House.” The administration has dismissed GAO opinions, arguing the agency has no authority over the executive branch because it is part of the legislative branch.

Democrats immediately denounced Ueland's nomination, saying it promised to further inflame tensions between the executive and legislative branches over the power of the purse.

“It would be lunacy for the Senate to hand a 15-year term leading Congress’ nonpartisan watchdog to a Russ Vought acolyte who spends his days plotting new ways for this administration to defy Congress," said Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., who is likely to chair the panel next year.

"Ueland orchestrated the president’s destructive mass firing campaign, is presiding over the razing of USAID, and is the last person who should be leading GAO," Murray mentioned in a statement.

In a recent development, sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., ranking member of the Homeland Security committee, urged all senators to oppose the Ueland nomination, saying it would provide “further power to the Executive Branch at a time when independent oversight from Congress is needed more than ever.”.

Peters also reiterated his previous criticism of Republicans for skipping bipartisan deliberations by a special 10-member legislative commission that is charged under statute with recommending candidates to the president for nomination.

“All three times the Commission process has occurred in the past, the president has selected a nominee with bipartisan support,” Peters noted.

In a sign of potential trouble for the nomination, a few Republicans expressed qualms about Ueland and what critics described as a rushed process for picking a GAO chief.

Sources indicate that "I'm not a fan," noted retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who faulted Ueland's boss for not providing proof of the cost savings claimed by Trump's Department of Government Efficiency, known as DOGE.

In a recent development, "To me, there's a lack of discipline or business experience in there to answer that simple question, or the reason they don't answer it is they don't have an answer," Tillis said. "Both are bad.".

While Tillis stopped short of promising to oppose Ueland, he mentioned the nomination "deserves individual consideration" instead of being taken up in a group with several other nominees.

And Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, "has concerns that the nomination is too partisan, particularly given how independent and long-term the appointment of the Comptroller General is," a spokesman said in a statement.

In a recent development, ueland has served as deputy director for management at the White House budget office since last year following his confirmation by the Senate on a party line 52-45 vote. He also has been performing the duties of the OMB controller since September 2025, according to his LinkedIn profile.

An expert on legislative procedure and strategy, Ueland has worked in a wide range of administrative and policy-oriented positions in the executive branch — including at OMB, the State Department and White House — and before that in the Senate.

He served as director of legislative affairs for Trump in his first term, as well as the State Department undersecretary for civilian security, democracy and human rights, and director of the department’s Office of U.S. Foreign Assistance, among other positions.

Sources indicate that before that, he was the Senate Budget Committee’s GOP staff director under then-Chairman Michael B. Enzi, R-Wyo., for four years through the end of 2017.

Earlier, he worked as chief of staff to then-Senate GOP Whip Don Nickles of Oklahoma and then-Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist of Tennessee.

Recent findings suggest that ueland, who has a bachelor’s degree in history from the University of San Francisco, lacks the financial background of recent past comptrollers. He has, however, gone deep in the weeds with numbers at OMB and the Senate Budget Committee, and has extensive experience as an administrator.

Former comptroller Charles A. Bowsher was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson and assistant secretary of the Navy for financial management before President Ronald Reagan tapped him to lead the GAO in 1981.

Recent findings suggest that david M. Walker, his successor, was a CPA, a partner at Arthur Anderson, assistant secretary of labor in the Employee Benefits Security Administration, and deputy executive director of the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation before his nomination by President Bill Clinton.

According to recent reports, gene L. Dodaro, whose 15-year term ended last year, had a bachelor’s degree in accounting and had worked at GAO for some 35 years before President Barack Obama nominated him to succeed Walker.

When Dodaro left, he designated Orice Williams Brown, who was GAO’s chief operating officer, as acting comptroller.

Sources indicate that before Trump nominated Ueland, the six Republican members of the legislative commission sent a letter to the White House last week recommending three candidates for the position — Ueland, Brian C. DeBusk and Roland Foster, according to sources.

In a recent development, deBusk is president and CEO of DeRoyal Industries, a privately held medical equipment manufacturer. He served on the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission from 2016 to 2022 after being appointed by Dodaro. Foster is a longtime GOP aide presently serving as senior adviser to retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa.

November 25: Uranus at opposition.

Industry observers note that celebrate Thanksgiving with a celestial turkey: The famous Orion Nebula (M42) is also playfully known as the Turkey Nebula because it looks to some like a turkey, particularly in deep astrophotos. But whether you’re a photographer or not, this bright deep-sky treat is easy to enjoy tonight while dinner digests.

Recent findings suggest that by about 9 P.M. local time, Orion the Hunter has risen above the eastern horizon, his recognizable three-star belt standing in a vertical line. The lowest star in that line is Alnitak (Zeta [ζ] Orionis), and the Orion Nebula lies just 3.7° south-southwest of this star, to its lower right on the sky this evening. You might be able to spot its glow without optical aid, although the bright Moon nearby may make that difficult. Binoculars or any telescope will easily show it.

Industry observers note that at 4th magnitude and spanning some 85’ by 60’, the Orion Nebula is a huge and bright star-forming region that sits roughly 1,350 light-years from Earth. In the brightest portion of the nebula lies a small grouping of young stars called the Trapezium Cluster. Take your time with this gorgeous sight, scanning around the region to pick out detail in the nebulosity. And if you are an astrophotographer, consider turning the view into a Thanksgiving memory to share for years to come.

Industry News: Nov. 26, 2018: Mars InSight lander touches down

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (380 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InSight, short for Interior Exploration using Seismic Investigations, Geodesy, and Heat Transport, landed on Mars Nov.
  • It has been revealed that in addition to bountiful seismic data, which included more than 1,300 marsquakes, InSight recorded about a year’s worth of weather data at the lander’s location with unprecedented accuracy, according to Bruce Banerdt, the mission’s principal investigator and principal research scientist.
  • It has been revealed that not everything was a rousing success, however.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InSight, short for Interior Exploration using Seismic Investigations, Geodesy, and Heat Transport, landed on Mars Nov. 26, 2018, tasked with a simple yet challenging mission: unlock the mysteries of Mars’ interior. Top priorities included uncovering Mars’ internal structure by measuring the thickness of the crust, obtaining the size and density of the core, and sussing out the structure and composition of Mars’ mantle.

It has been revealed that in addition to bountiful seismic data, which included more than 1,300 marsquakes, InSight recorded about a year’s worth of weather data at the lander’s location with unprecedented accuracy, according to Bruce Banerdt, the mission’s principal investigator and principal research scientist. The InSight lander also took the first magnetic field measurements on the surface of Mars and measured several properties of the soil around it.

It has been revealed that not everything was a rousing success, however. Most famously, the mission’s “mole” subsurface probe only penetrated about 16 inches (40 centimeters) deep, despite being designed to burrow to a depth of at least 3 feet (10 meters). It turned out that the soil beneath InSight’s struts was unlike any previously encountered on the surface; it simply didn’t cooperate with the instrument’s design. But even that cloud has a silver lining, as it provided scientists with key details about the terrain upon which InSight landed.

InSight’s successful initial two-year mission was extended to run at least through the end of December 2022. But the stationary lander relied on power generated from its two large solar panels, which steadily gathered dust. That dust reduced the panels’ efficiency over time, forcing mission planners to make tough choices regarding power allotment. In May of 2022, engineers placed the craft’s robotic arm into a final resting pose and turned off all its instruments, save one: InSight’s seismometer continued to operate on what little power was available, running about half the time, according to Banerdt. InSight last contacted Earth Dec. 15, 2022, after which two attempts were made to raise the lander. Both failed, and a few days later, NASA officially brought the mission to a close.

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

This man sometimes sees his cat’s eyes on people’s faces

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • It has been revealed that after returning home from a 2024 brain surgery, a man started noticing something strange: Eyes that he had previously seen started showing up on the face he was right now looking at.
  • In a recent development, “Right when I got home from the hospitals, I was seeing my cat in my mother and my sister,” says the 29-year-old teacher, who has asked to go by Karl to protect his privacy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It has been revealed that after returning home from a 2024 brain surgery, a man started noticing something strange: Eyes that he had previously seen started showing up on the face he was right now looking at. To his bewilderment, the swapping of features even extended to his pet cat Luna.

In a recent development, “Right when I got home from the hospitals, I was seeing my cat in my mother and my sister,” says the 29-year-old teacher, who has asked to go by Karl to protect his privacy. “That was one of the first things that I noticed,” he says. “And the cat even took on resemblances of people.”.

Industry observers note that it was unsettling, to say the least. “Looking at her and then looking at somebody else, I might see her giant eyes on a person.”.

Scientists have now described Karl’s perception of faces in the December concern of Cortex. His condition, in which echoes of a previously viewed image appear in a latest context, is called palinopsia, and it was likely caused by Karl’s brain surgery. Because the echoes appear on faces, they distort how faces look to him, a condition known as prosopometamorphopsia. The new work offers clues about how brains perceive faces, both under normal and unusual conditions.

In a recent development, the researchers’ analyses of the man’s face perceptions are “wonderfully innovative,” says clinical psychiatrist Jan Dirk Blom of Leiden University and Parnassia Psychiatric Institute in the Netherlands, who was not involved in the work. “In this era of big data and complex statistical analyses, we almost forget how informative clinical observations in single patients can be.”.

Karl’s unusual perceptions caught the attention of researchers. “His face processing system is disrupted, and it’s disrupted in a specific way,” says Brad Duchaine, a visual neuroscientist at Dartmouth University. “For reasons we don’t understand, items from memory are being pulled up and pasted onto the face that he’s perceiving.”.

According to recent reports, duchaine’s lab has been collecting case studies of people who perceive faces differently in an effort to learn about visual perception. Duchaine and his colleagues assessed Karl’s experiences by showing him images of faces and asking him to describe what he saw. This confirmed that he consistently saw distortions in the eye regions of faces, such as the shape, and in faces’ shading and sometimes even texture. As they worked together, Duchaine and Karl used AI-image generators to create pictures of faces that resemble what Karl saw for the cat-human swap.

Karl isn’t the only person with palinopsia that affects faces, Duchaine claims. A few other people have contacted him who also see echoes of prior faces. But Karl’s palinopsia seems different. “His were really consistent, very long-lasting. And then the cross-species transfer is something that I’d never heard before,” with one major exception, Duchaine says. A case study from 1986 describes a woman who, after seeing a poodle on a bus, saw poodle heads on every other passenger, too. That woman’s distortions lasted only about half an hour; Karl’s perceptual shifts have been consistently present since his 2024 surgery.

Recent findings suggest that “What is latest about the present study is the finding that a cat’s eyes can apparently be transposed from memory banks onto human faces observed in the here and now, and vice versa,” says Blom. “And that we now have a rough idea of the brain areas making this possible.”.

According to recent reports, during a surgery to correct malformed blood vessels, doctors removed tissue from Karl’s right posterior temporal area, a part of the brain known to be involved in face recognition. Karl’s experiences hint at how the visual system detects and interprets features on faces, Duchaine states. There’s an idea that humans interpret faces holistically, as a single object, he says. Karl’s case highlights some of the limits of this idea, because he’s having these effects specific to the eye region, Duchaine says.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s sort of like a filter,” Karl says, describing his experience of palinopsia. “It decides on a style, and then that style is applied to everyone in my reality, including myself.” These filters can change across a day or last several weeks, Karl says. He’s even experienced eye feature swaps from a face he saw in a dream. “And that was then applied to me, looking in a mirror, and then everybody else.”Karl also experiences echoes of environments, he says. For instance, if he has visited an area with lots of potholes in the roads, visual echoes of those potholes can appear in a newer road. A similar thing can happen with shapes, he says: Echoes of square hallways or stairwells can appear in new spots.

According to recent reports, using AI and collaboration to help re-create what Karl sees is an advance, Blom states. And this sort of collaboration between scientist and volunteer is crucial. “In my line of work, clinical psychiatry, we know that everything stands and falls with the descriptions that our patients give us,” he says. “In my opinion, this is patient participation at its best.”.

#226248. The closest exoplanets may host magnetic fields

The closest exoplanets may host magnetic fields

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1416 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In all the universe, Earth is the only planet known to have life.
  • Sources indicate that but Earth is far from the only planet we know of.
  • Sources indicate that because of their protective role, magnetic fields have major implications in the search for life beyond Earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In all the universe, Earth is the only planet known to have life. A big part of the reason life is possible here is our planet’s magnetic field. It acts like a shield, deflecting harmful energy from our Sun as well as cosmic rays from deep space that could otherwise erode Earth’s atmosphere and irradiate the surface, a death sentence for evolving life-forms.

Sources indicate that but Earth is far from the only planet we know of. As of this writing, there are more than 6,300 confirmed exoplanets on the roster, with more added by the day. Scientists have discovered stars with as many planets as our own Sun hosts. In other systems, planets as big as Jupiter whip around their sun in only a few days’ time. Astronomers have even discovered planets that orbit multiple stars at once, and they recently caught a glimpse of a possible atmosphere around a rocky, Earth-sized world in its star’s habitable zone. But until 2026, they had no compelling evidence that any terrestrial exoplanets had magnetic fields of their own.

Sources indicate that because of their protective role, magnetic fields have major implications in the search for life beyond Earth. Astronomers have long suspected that part of the reason Mars now appears dead is that its magnetic field fizzled out billions of years ago. This let the solar wind strip the water and other volatile compounds from its atmosphere, leaving it cold and barren.

Sources indicate that beyond the solar system, in 2019 researchers reported “indirect detections of exoplanetary magnetic fields” in four hot Jupiters. Then, a 2021 study found a strong signature of a magnetic field around HAT-P-11 b, a Neptune-like planet. Two years later, a pair of studies detected possible signs of a magnetic field around YZ Ceti b — this time, a rocky, Earth-like planet roughly the same size as, and only a bit less massive than our own. But this find has not yet been confirmed.

Sources indicate that in July 2026, a study published in Astronomy & Astrophysics found possible evidence of magnetic fields around two rocky exoplanets. Not just any exoplanets, either — Proxima Centauri b and d, the closest confirmed planets beyond our solar system, orbiting the red dwarf Proxima Centauri 4.2 light-years away.

Recent findings suggest that proxima b, roughly Earth’s mass and size, orbits every 11.1 days. Proxima d, likely a quarter to a third of our planet’s mass and 70% its size, orbits closer in with a period of 5.1 days. Because Proxima Centauri is smaller and less massive than our Sun, Proxima b is inside the habitable zone, where temperatures allow liquid surface water. A third planet, Proxima c, was tentatively detected in 2019 but is still unconfirmed. Astronomers don’t yet know if any of these worlds host atmospheres.

According to recent reports, the latest study, led by María Rosa Zapatero Osorio of the Centro de Astrobiología in Madrid, Spain, used 117 separate observations made with the Echelle SPectrograph for Rocky Exoplanets and Stable Spectroscopic Observations (ESPRESSO) instrument on the Very Large Telescope atop Cerro Paranal in Chile. The research followed up on previous studies conducted with ESPRESSO in 2020 and 2022, which focused on confirming the presence of planets around Proxima Centauri. Zapatero Osorio and her collaborators used the data to identify a peculiar correlation between the timing of flares emitted from Proxima Centauri and the orbital periods of its planets.

Industry observers note that “We detected low-energy flares occurring with a characteristic period of about 5.1 days,” Zapatero Osorio states. “This is very close to Proxima d’s orbital period.” But flares did not occur during every orbit of Proxima d, so the team ran statistical analyses to determine whether the flares were preferentially occurring at particular phases of the planet’s orbit. They found strong statistical evidence “that the occurrence of the flares is not randomly distributed over the planet’s orbital period,” Zapatero Osorio says. “Instead, a significant number of flares tend to occur at particular times in Proxima d’s orbit.” This is a possible indication that Proxima d could be interacting magnetically with its parent star, which would be likely to happen if the planet has a strong magnetic field of its own.

According to recent reports, using a model adapted from the physics of solar flares, Zapatero Osorio’s team calculated that Proxima d could have a magnetic field anywhere from 8 to 230 gauss in strength, with the best median estimate limited to around 16 gauss. This is about 27 times more powerful than Earth’s magnetic field (0.6 gauss), which protects life on Earth from the worst of the Sun’s energy.

Their model assumes that the star and planet are magnetically connected, Zapatero Osorio indicates. Each sustains its own magnetic field, and these fields are interconnected. As a result of this connection, stress builds up on the stellar surface. From time to time, this stress is released in the form of low-energy flares, whose period is closely tied to the planet’s orbital period.

Although there was not as strong a correlation between Proxima b’s orbital period and the stellar flares, the team did find that Proxima b could also be interacting with the star, albeit in a lesser capacity. This suggests that although the finding is less sure, Proxima b may also sustain a magnetic field.

Industry observers note that there are alternative explanations for the findings. One possibility is that there could be intrinsic, long-lived active regions on Proxima Centauri itself that account for the peculiar timing of the flares. Another explanation is that gravitational interactions between the planets and Proxima Centauri could induce disturbances on the star without requiring a strong planetary magnetosphere, although the team suggests this is less likely. It’s also possible that when Proxima’s stellar wind reaches the planets, it interacts with them in a way that mimics the effects of a planetary magnetic field without requiring one.

It has been revealed that like most red dwarfs, Proxima is a highly active star, regularly belching out intense flares that would be hazardous to any fledgling life-forms on the worlds in close orbit. Because Proxima is so close to Earth and has at least one rocky planet in its habitable zone, it makes a perfect testbed for studying how stellar flares could affect habitability around red dwarfs — the most common stars in the universe.

Astronomers looking for habitable worlds around these stars must contend with the likelihood that any planets would be effectively sterilized by the intense radiation in the flares constantly washing over them. Now, though, there is a glimmer of hope. If Proxima b and d do have magnetic fields, as this research suggests, they could act much like Earth’s own protective magnetic shield, deflecting enough harmful stellar radiation that life might just be able to take hold.

Recent findings suggest that “Earth’s magnetic field plays an notable role in protecting life and supporting human progress,” says Zapatero Osorio. “It shields our planet from the solar wind and energetic particles, and it has also played an important role in navigation.”.

Sources indicate that unfortunately, Proxima d is so close to its host star that it is likely too hot to sustain life as we know it. Proxima b, however, lies within the habitable zone. “Based on the results of our study, both Proxima d and b may have magnetospheres capable of providing some protection against their host star’s activity,” Zapatero Osorio says.

According to recent reports, the importance of this find goes deeper than simply a pair of neighboring planets. In the last few years, evidence has emerged that gas giant exoplanets similar to Jupiter and Saturn host magnetic fields. These are the easiest types of planets to detect and study, but while magnetic fields around such worlds are certainly fascinating, the implications for planetary habitability are limited.

But as the number of known planets continues to swell, so, too, does our sample of Earth-like worlds. And if the two closest rocky planets beyond our solar system do indeed have magnetic fields, then perhaps these features are common. If true, it increases the chances that rocky worlds across the galaxy could be habitable — at least, for life-forms as we understand them. And the more planets capable of hosting life, the more likely it is that we might someday discover we are not alone.

Nick Oakes is a science writer for NASA’s Heliophysics Education Activation Team at Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland.

Newly introduced aviation funding request hits Senate turbulence

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (912 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov.
  • Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.
  • Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov. 10. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.

Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.

“I got to obviously see the explanation behind it, or sort of laying out the numbers why it's necessary,” Thune mentioned of the $50 billion, which jumped from $30 billion a day earlier.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters he was unimpressed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s request and that he wanted to see a breakdown of how the department would use the funds.

“They got to give us an update,” Tillis stated. “I mean, the $50 billion request — I thought that was $30 billion. So people have got to explain to me, really, even the basis for the $30 billion, let alone the additional $20 billion that Duffy mentioned the other day.”.

Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., similarly noted legislators would need “more detail” on the request but said “obviously there needs to be more” funding for the modernization efforts.

Hoeven serves on the Senate Transportation-HUD Appropriations Subcommittee, which rolled out a fiscal 2027 spending bill Monday that would increase the FAA’s annual allocation to facilities and equipment by $500 million, a nearly 13 percent boost.

Duffy is slotted to attend the Senate GOP conference lunch on Tuesday, where he is likely to be peppered with such requests for specifics. Meanwhile, FAA staff are expected to brief House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee aides on Tuesday, after that meeting got pushed on Monday.

The Senate’s go-slow approach is in contrast to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who said over the weekend that he would add the $50 billion request to a year-end legislative package.

The White House’s call for additional funds ballooned last week in the aftermath of the nationwide ground stop that created confusion and concern at airports around the country. The Federal Aviation Administration remarked Sunday that the unusual move was made “out of an abundance of caution” after legacy equipment became flooded with data during routine upgrades.

The FAA’s initial investigation tied the data flooding to work being done at a radar site in Texas and a radio communications site in Arkansas by contractor L3Harris Technologies.

Speaking on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Duffy stated the server thought to have caused the flooding was taken to the L3Harris lab in Florida where FAA personnel are working with the FBI to analyze the router that likely caused the system instability.

Still, as administration officials attempt to understand the system errors that led to the ground stop, Duffy has used the moment as justification to lobby for additional funds.

“In this old telecom network, I do have money to switch over from the old copper wires to fiber and we’re 70 percent completed with that mission, but we need a brand newly introduced architecture for our telecom and aviation,” Duffy said on CNBC Monday. “This can happen promptly to build a new state of the art telecom network, it’s just that it has to be funded.”.

A day before the incident, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought wrote to congressional appropriators, formally asking for $30.1 billion in added funds for the modernization effort, in line with a bill introduced by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., in late September. That ask inexplicably jumped up to $50 billion by Friday night in the aftermath of the ground stop.

On Monday, Thune noted the prior request for approximately $30 billion, which he stated included “some other stuff” as well.

Schmitt’s bill and the White House request would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $7.2 billion for a “common automation platform and a common controller workstation,” and $2 billion for cloud computing and telecommunications infrastructure.

Another $10 billion would go toward airport improvement projects, including $2 billion to “construct, replace, and improve terminal air traffic control facilities, including activities using digital tower technologies.”.

The request includes $10 billion for a terminal modernization or reconstruction pilot program for certain midsized airports.

Thune said Monday that he tallied about $12 billion in the fresh request specifically for air traffic control related issues, likely a reference to the $10.1 billion plus the $2 billion for terminal facilities.

According to recent reports, “I think there's more we need to figure out, and obviously I think we all agree that we need to be modernizing and updating, particularly in an area like that where safety is the number one priority, but also we want to do that in a smart way and make sure that we're using taxpayer dollars wisely and well,” Thune mentioned. “We’ll hear him out.”.

Meanwhile, Democrats kept up the drumbeat of criticism, both for the airspace management that led to the ground stop and the rollout of the fresh funding request.

“So typical of this incompetent administration — they have money, they don’t use it and then they come back and say ‘give us more money,'” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., remarked on the floor.

Savannah Behrmann and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#226242. The Sky This Week from November 27 to December 4: Brilliant Venus

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1990 w)

The Sky This Week from November 27 to December 4: Brilliant Venus

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1990 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Friday, November 27As fall deepens and winter approaches, the wintertime star patterns are reappearing in our evening sky.
  • In a recent development, look east late tonight to locate the waning gibbous Moon near the border of Gemini and Cancer.
  • Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (82%) *Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Friday, November 27As fall deepens and winter approaches, the wintertime star patterns are reappearing in our evening sky. One is a large asterism called the Winter Hexagon, now fully above the horizon by about 10 P.M. local time. You should be able to spot this shape even with the Moon nearby, as each point in the Winter Hexagon is a bright, well-known star.

In a recent development, look east late tonight to locate the waning gibbous Moon near the border of Gemini and Cancer. This will help you find the first point in the Hexagon, the pair of stars Castor and Pollux, the heads of Gemini the Twins, glowing just above the Moon at this time. From there, look upward for another bright star in neighboring Auriga — this is Capella, the next point in the Hexagon. From Capella, look left and down just a little to find the V-shaped face of Taurus the Bull, where the bright star Aldebaran shines, marking the next point. Then it’s down to Orion’s bright knee, Rigel, before you drop down and a little left, close to the horizon, to land on Sirius, the brightest star in the sky and the nose of Canis Major. The Hexagon closes out with the luminary of the Little Dog, Procyon.

Sunrise: 6:59 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 7:53 P.M. Moonset: 10:26 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (82%) *Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Sources indicate that saturday, November 28Saturn remains a bright naked-eye object all evening, setting around 2 A.M. local time. Around 8 P.M., you’ll find it high in the south, to the left of the Circlet of Pisces and above the body of Cetus the Whale.

Tonight and for the next few nights, Saturn’s strange, two-faced moon Iapetus is skimming north of the planet, making it easier to find. Now glowing at 11th magnitude, it is heading west toward a late December western elongation, when it will shine about a magnitude brighter but sit far from Saturn. Once you’ve got Saturn in your scope, look about 2’ northeast to land on Iapetus. Over the next few nights, it will move westward, reaching inferior conjunction and standing due north of the ringed world by the 30th.

If you can catch 11th-magnitude Iapetus, you’ll also see four brighter moons: 10th-magnitude Dione, Rhea, and Tethys closer to Saturn; and mid-8th-magnitude Titan, about 3’ to Saturn’s west. The latter is the planet’s largest and brightest moon, easy to spot in any size scope and often even binoculars. If you keep returning each night to track Iapetus, also keep an eye on Titan, which is moving eastward toward the planet and will pass south of Saturn on December 2. Dione, Rhea, and Tethys have smaller orbits and shorter periods, so they move visibly over the course of several hours, frequently swapping places and passing in front of or behind Saturn. For example, Dione disappears behind Saturn’s southwestern limb in an occultation around 12:20 A.M. EST on the 29th (still late on the 28th in time zones farther west).

Sunrise: 7:00 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 9:10 P.M. Moonset: 11:09 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (73%).

Industry observers note that sunday, November 29Have you ever seen your shadow by planetlight? Venus reaches greatest brilliancy at 2 P.M. EST, now shining at magnitude –4.9. Rising nearly three and a half hours before the Sun, Venus will be so bright that it could potentially cast a shadow if you’re in a location with particularly dark skies (Bortle 1 or 2).

Even without perfect viewing conditions, this morning star can’t be missed. By an hour before sunrise, Venus is roughly 25° high in the southeast, blazing just to the lower left of Spica, the brightest star in Virgo. Far to Venus’ lower left, closer to the ground, Mercury stands nearly 5° above the horizon, shining at magnitude –0.7.

Sources indicate that compare the two planets through a telescope. Venus is a 27%-lit crescent, but its disk stretches 40” across. Mercury, by comparison, is much smaller, just 6” across, but its phase is 82%. Now through the first week of December is the best time to catch the solar system’s smallest planet, as it remains bright but appears to sink toward the horizon day by day. By the 5th, Mercury will be less than 2° high an hour before sunrise, making viewing challenging both because of potential obstacles on the horizon as well as the more turbulent layer of air near the ground.

Venus, meanwhile, stays at roughly the same altitude an hour before sunrise all month, its phase growing to nearly 50% lit by the end of the year. Earth’s sister planet will remain prominent in the morning sky through the first half of next year.

Sunrise: 7:01 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 10:25 P.M. Moonset: 11:43 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (62%).

Industry observers note that monday, November 30Venus remains a brilliant and unmissable morning star, but it’s not the only object worth paying attention to before dawn. Leo is hosting a celestial get-together this morning as the Moon joins two planets and the star that sits at the heart of the Lion, just beneath the Sickle asterism.

In a recent development, the waning gibbous Moon is the brightest object here; next brightest is Jupiter, located to the Moon’s upper right and glowing at magnitude –2.2. The gas giant stands nearly side by side with Mars (to Jupiter’s left); the Red Planet is fainter but still a respectable magnitude 0.4. Both planets are slowly growing in brightness and size as they approach opposition early next year. Through a telescope, Jupiter stretches 39” across, offering excellent views of its alternating light and dark cloud bands, and Mars is now 8” wide.

Sources indicate that shining between Mars and the Moon is 1st-magnitude Regulus, often drawn as both the heart of Leo and the base of the Sickle asterism’s handle. The curving backward question mark of stars that forms the Sickle’s blade and the Lion’s head in profile lies above the grouping in the sky before dawn.

Sliding along the ecliptic, the Moon passes 1.2° south of Jupiter at 4 A.M. EST, then 1.1° south of Regulus at 10 A.M. EST and 3° south of Mars at 3 P.M. EST.

According to recent reports, sunrise: 7:02 A.M. Sunset: 4:35 P.M. Moonrise: 11:36 P.M. Moonset: 12:11 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (51%).

Industry observers note that tuesday, December 1Last Quarter Moon occurs at 1:09 A.M. EST. A few hours later, asteroid 2 Pallas reaches a stationary point at 7 A.M. EST. Located in Cetus, it is visible all evening, setting around 1 A.M. local time. It stands highest around 8 P.M., when it’s roughly 30° above the southern horizon, about 4.2° southeast of 2nd-magnitude Diphda (Beta [β] Ceti).

Industry observers note that glowing at magnitude 9.0, Pallas is easy to find with a small scope. It sits near a neat triangle of 5th- to 6th-magnitude stars, which lie about 1.5° southwest of the asteroid and act as a great reference point to find it tonight. Pallas is 1° east of the easternmost star. Previously, Pallas was closing on that star, moving westward. But after tonight, it will turn and move slowly eastward again, pulling away from the little triangle night by night.

Sources indicate that drop about 5° south of this region for an added treat: 8th-magnitude globular cluster NGC 288, just over the celestial border in Sculptor. Spanning about 13’, this ancient ball of stars lies nearly 49,000 light-years away. It’s also near another deep-sky target, the 7th-magnitude galaxy NGC 253. Often called the Silver Coin or Sculptor Galaxy, this stunning edge-on spiral lies about 1.7° northwest of NGC 288 and can be viewed together with the cluster in wide-field instruments such as binoculars or finder scopes.

Sources indicate that sunrise: 7:03 A.M. Sunset: 4:35 P.M. Moonrise: — Moonset: 12:35 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (40%).

In a recent development, wednesday, December 2It’s now asteroid 4 Vesta’s turn to reach a stationary point at 11 A.M. EST as it, too, swims through the domain of Cetus the Whale. Visible in the evening sky, Vesta sits more than 40° above the southern horizon around 7 P.M. local time. Previously moving retrograde, or westward, it will now begin moving prograde, or eastward, against the background stars.

This month Vesta is located roughly halfway between bright Saturn to its northwest and magnitude 3.6 Theta (θ) Ceti to its southeast. Saturn is impossible to miss, as it’s the brightest object in this region of the sky. To locate 7th-magnitude Vesta, find Saturn early in the evening and slide about 8.1° east-southeast to land on the main-belt world. There aren’t a lot of background stars in the immediate vicinity, so try to match your view to the star chart above to locate the asteroid in your eyepiece. Because it’s moving slowly, you’ll need to come back every night or two to check out the view and note the light that’s shifted position — that’s Vesta.

Sunrise: 7:04 A.M. Sunset: 4:35 P.M. Moonrise: 12:43 A.M. Moonset: 12:58 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (30%).

According to recent reports, thursday, December 3Look north a few hours after sunset to find the W-shaped star pattern of Cassiopeia on her head, looking more like the letter M as this circumpolar constellation swings above the North Celestial Pole. Just 1.9° northwest of Navi (Gamma [γ] Cassiopeiae), the midpoint of the M (or W), is a lovely open cluster cataloged as NGC 225 and known as the Sailboat Cluster.

According to recent reports, longtime Astronomy contributor Rod Pommier gave the cluster its nickname because he saw an arc of stars within the cluster that looked to him like the sail of a boat catching the wind, connected to a straight line of stars forming the mast and another eight stars outlining the vessel itself. The stars of the cluster are roughly 2,100 light-years distant, and this grouping was discovered by Caroline Herschel in 1783.

For added visual interest, the cluster is set against a complex of dark nebulae made of dust, which block the starlight behind them.

Sunrise: 7:05 A.M. Sunset: 4:35 P.M. Moonrise: 1:49 A.M. Moonset: 1:20 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (21%).

Friday, December 4The waning Moon puts even faint deep-sky objects within reach on these early December evenings. Tonight, let’s look toward a distant elliptical galaxy nestled in the far southeastern corner of Lacerta the Lizard. Cataloged as NGC 7426, this 13th-magnitude stellar smudge sits close to a lovely pair of contrasting stars, making finding it a rewarding sight for all: While you do need a larger scope to track down the galaxy, the stars are visible even through smaller instruments, offering something for everyone.

Around 7 P.M. tonight, our target is still more than 35° high in the west. The zig-zagging figure of Lacerta sits just above cross-shaped Cygnus as the Summer Triangle sinks toward the western horizon. To Lacerta’s left (southeast) is Pegasus, and we’ll use 3rd-magnitude Matar (Eta [η] Pegasi) as our jumping-off point. From here, slide about 5° north-northeast to find a pair of stars, 6th and 8th magnitude, roughly 1’ apart. The brighter star glows blue-white, while its dimmer neighbor shines orangey-gold. NGC 7426 lies roughly 4’ east-northeast of this pair, appearing as a faint, grayish-white smudge. It measures roughly 2’ by 1.5’, its compact size helping to keep its faint light confined to a relatively small area.

Sources indicate that sunrise: 7:06 A.M. Sunset: 4:34 P.M. Moonrise: 2:54 A.M. Moonset: 1:44 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (14%).

Industry observers note that alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

Latest Update: Extinct, long-legged grasshoppers walked on water alongside dinosaurs
